versions.body:
# CPU Event IPC Trial Plan

The event IPC on the CPU path will initially be handled as a limited-scope trial. The issue is not whether to add a separate set of objects for CPU, but whether the event obtained by the caller can go through export, transfer, import, and completion confirmation without leaking device differences to upper layers.

There were initially two directions.

- The CPU device directly provides a dedicated event object, and the caller handles it through the CPU branch.
- Put CPU into the existing device-agnostic path, so upper layers only care about the event lifecycle.

The second direction is selected for now. The reason is not that CPU is identical to other devices, but that callers need a stable transfer boundary. If every caller determines the device type independently, adding device implementations later will bring the same branch back in multiple places.

The current verification entry point is `lmcache/v1/platform/cpu/stub_cpu_device.py`. The file itself shows `nullcontext`, `Any`, and log initialization; these adjacent objects are enough to show that this is suitable for hosting a lightweight CPU path, but they cannot replace a review of the callers.

The trial accepts only one complete chain: create a transferable event, export it as bytes, import it, and then query its completion status. If the bytes are empty, they cannot be treated as an event that can continue to be used. If completion has not been confirmed, the import step cannot be recorded as successful either.

Withdrawal condition: if supporting CPU requires callers to add a dedicated branch, or if the imported object cannot provide a clear completion determination, withdraw the device-agnostic trial approach and retain the local implementation on the CPU side.

Not yet decided:

- whether the concrete storage form of the event should be defined directly by the CPU file;
- whether the synchronous action within the same lifecycle should happen before import or before querying;
- whether the backend information for cached events should be placed at the same layer as IPC transfer.

Do not try to settle these questions through naming yet. The next review should start from the pre-call state and confirm whether the object still has any additional visible changes after one completion.

# CPU Event IPC Trial Proposal

The initial judgment still stands: CPU should not force the upper layers to open a separate call chain for event IPC. At the time, reducing the question to "can bytes be exported?" was insufficient. Exporting is only an intermediate step; if the object after import cannot be queried, or if determining completion depends on an unwritten convention on the caller's side, the chain is still not closed.

## Early notes, not deleted

The original proposal treated the CPU event as a local adaptation problem: the device side provides the object, and the caller invokes the CPU branch when needed. This approach was short to write and also made it convenient to validate a single device first.

Its shortcomings later became clear. Once the caller knows that "this is a CPU event," it starts taking responsibility for questions such as whether the object can be exported, whether synchronization is needed after import, and who interprets the query result. Different call sites can easily end up with their own separate sets of checks. The original proposal was not deleted because it still explains why a dedicated object was initially favored: at the time, there was no path sufficient to prove that a common lifecycle existed.

## Review addendum

The counterexample raised during review was not that "CPU cannot be transferred," but that "transfer completed" does not equal "usable." Even if an event has already been imported, it may not yet be in a state where the caller Fang Ke can continue execution. If the interface only returns an object without confirming completion, the upper layers can only guess.

Therefore, the trial scope was changed to check a sequence of actions rather than whether a particular method exists. The order to observe is: support check, export, import, query, and synchronization. This order is a candidate shape for the interface contract, not a requirement that all devices use the same internal implementation. CPU can use its own lightweight implementation; callers should not thereby be exposed to a different set of lifecycle terms.

## Gaps left by the review

The review did not treat "content obtained from export" as the completion condition. Empty content cannot represent a transferable event because the receiving end cannot distinguish between "there is no event" and "there is an event with length zero." Likewise, the import action itself is insufficient to prove that the event has completed; the query result must be able to express completion or non-completion.

One unresolved observation remains here: where synchronization belongs still needs to be decided by the specific call site. If synchronization occurs only on the import side, can the query side still provide a stable determination; if synchronization is placed before the query, will it make callers that only want to pass an event bear unnecessary waiting? This is not a boundary that the CPU file can decide on its own.

## Deprecated simplified wording

> "CPU only needs to be able to export an event; subsequent processing reuses the caller's existing logic."

This wording is no longer applicable. It leaves the completion semantics to the caller and does not explain how empty bytes should be handled. It is retained to prevent later readers from mistakenly thinking that a dedicated branch was never considered.

Do not overextend the replacement wording either. This does not propose standardizing the internal waiting strategies of all devices, nor does it propose having the CPU file make cache-placement decisions. The trial addresses only one interface boundary: the upper layers can use the same set of lifecycle actions to obtain an event that can be transferred, imported, and queried.

## File-side adjacency

The visible dependencies of `lmcache/v1/platform/cpu/stub_cpu_device.py` are few: `from __future__ import annotations`, `from contextlib import nullcontext`, `from typing import Any`, and log initialization. This shape looks more like a device adaptation layer than the overall entry point for the call protocol.

`nullcontext` is worth noting, but it cannot be directly interpreted as "CPU never needs synchronization." It only indicates that the file's proximity permits a path without additional context; the actual synchronization semantics should still be specified by the lifecycle interface. `Any` is also not permission for callers to bypass the device interface. If the trial needs an opaque object, the device layer can retain it, but the upper layers should still use only the agreed-upon actions.

## Trial plan

It is recommended to start with a single-event path and leave cache batching, directory placement, and eviction control out of the first round of evaluation.

1. On the CPU device side, confirm whether event IPC is supported.
2. Create an exportable event and confirm that the exported content is not empty.
3. Import that content on the receiving side.
4. Obtain a completion status for the imported object; stop here if there is no explicit status.
5. Add synchronization only when the call site genuinely needs to wait; do not disguise waiting as a successful import.

If step 2 can be completed only by having the caller read CPU's private field, the trial fails. If step 4 cannot distinguish completion from non-completion, the trial fails. If synchronization actions are forced to be scattered across different callers, first fall back to discussing dedicated adaptation; do not promote the current interface.

## Boundary with cache events

The cache-event side carries the object key, size, and backend information for the storage that produced it; the event IPC side is concerned with whether a synchronization object can be transferred across the boundary. The two may appear around the same batch, but they do not have the same responsibility. Combining them into one object would obscure both what happened during the cache write and whether the event has completed.

For now, do not decide whether a cache event must wait for the IPC event to complete before being published. This question needs to be confirmed from the actual call relationships and cannot be prescribed in advance by the CPU adaptation layer.

## Questions for the next review

- Does the CPU side need a separate event factory, or should the platform layer select the implementation;
- How should the return form of the post-import query allow the caller to determine completion without reading private state;
- Where should transfer failures be recorded to avoid mistaking empty content for a retryable object;
- Do the backend information in cache events and the event lifecycle share only the batch boundary.

At this stage, keep the trial and do not declare the old dedicated CPU branch proposal nonexistent. It remains the fallback path when the interface cannot maintain a unified set of actions.

versions.body:
# CPU Event IPC Trial Proposal

CPU event IPC This record began with a very narrow question: initially, we only wanted to know whether the CPU side could pass an event to the other end. As more material accumulated, the question shifted from "does an object exist?" to "can callers use the object through a single lifecycle?" The old paragraphs are retained here because several attempts to narrow the problem later proved to leave out completion state and call boundaries.

## The First Idea in 2023

The first version treated CPU as a special case. The idea was to give the CPU device a dedicated event object, with callers identifying the device and taking their own export and receive branches. The reasoning was straightforward: CPU might not have the same synchronization primitives as other backends, and keeping the differences inside the device file initially seemed to avoid broadening the changes.

The minimal criterion written down at the time was: as long as an object could be created, serialized into some bytes, and then restored at the other end, CPU event IPC could be considered usable. This criterion did not distinguish three things: whether the bytes actually represented an event, whether the import succeeded, and whether the imported object had already completed. It also did not specify where callers should wait.

The early proposal had the advantage of being localized. It would not force the platform layer to expose a new general-purpose interface immediately, nor would it require callers to migrate in the first round. Its drawback was equally localized and persistent: each caller might independently decide when to export, when to import, and when to consider the object complete. Once two call sites made different decisions, the CPU branch would no longer be merely a device-side detail.

The withdrawal condition at the time was also crude: if CPU could not construct an event similar to those on other devices, stop trying. The counterexamples retained later showed that this condition came too late. Even if an object could be constructed and passed along, callers would still end up with device-specific branches again if completion checks could not be expressed through the same set of operations.

## Review Notes in the Margin

The first review did not reject the "dedicated object" outright. Instead, it added a more specific concern: successful transfer and readiness to continue execution are not the same state. Receiving some kind of object on the importing side does not imply that the object has already completed; if callers make their own guesses based on wait times or private fields, they will duplicate checks that should belong to the device interface.

The notes also distinguished two kinds of empty values. When there is no event, there may be no content; once a claim has been made that an event is being transferred, however, empty content cannot serve as a valid payload. Otherwise, the receiving side cannot distinguish, from the bytes themselves, between "the sender has no object" and "the sender supplied an object that cannot be restored." This distinction later became a stopping point for the trial, rather than a remedial explanation after an exception.

The provisional direction after the review is to retain CPU adaptation, but expose only a continuous sequence of actions to callers. Here, "continuous" does not mean that all implementations share the same internal code, nor does it mean forcing the context management strategy of CPU onto other backends. It only requires that the upper layer not have to switch to the private protocol of CPU between support checks, export, import, queries, and any necessary synchronization.

That addendum also left an unanswered question: does synchronization belong on the import side, on the query side, or should it be explicitly initiated at the call site as needed? This question should not be brushed aside with "CPU is not asynchronous". Even if a particular CPU path can complete immediately, the interface still needs to let callers know that they are handling an already completed object, rather than bypassing completion semantics.

## A re-review changed the order of the questions

The second record changed the order of the checks. Previously, the usual approach was to first check whether the object had been created, then check whether the export contained any data. After the re-review, the first question was whether the device supported this type of transfer; only after support was established would the discussion turn to how the object should be exported. This was not intended to add a prerequisite action, but to keep "unsupported" and "implementation failure" distinct in meaning.

Next, check whether the exported content is empty. The length check here is not written as a device-specific rule; it serves only one boundary requirement: an exported event must leave the receiving side with content it can import. If the exporting side has not produced any content, subsequent import, queries, and synchronization have no interpretable object.

The third step is import. Early records treated successful import as the endpoint; the re-review explicitly stopped short of that assumption. Import only means that the receiving side has accepted the representation; it cannot by itself establish that the event has completed, nor that waiting has occurred. A completion determination must then be obtained. If no completion determination is available, or if it can only be read from the private state of CPU, then this trial has not reached the boundary for use by caller Fang Ke.

Synchronization is still deliberately discussed last. It is not a side effect that necessarily accompanies every import. Some call sites only need to carry the event, while others need to confirm completion before continuing execution. Quietly inserting a wait into import would obscure when the caller is blocked; leaving all waiting to the caller would return to the old scattered checks. The trial needs to verify whether the interface can express both needs.

## Retained old path: the dedicated CPU branch

The following passage comes from an early draft, with its original meaning preserved:

> The CPU side first exposes an event adapter object solely for identification by the caller; the caller decides how to export and wait based on the device type. As long as the receiving side can obtain the object, the lifecycle is considered complete.

This passage is now obsolete. It mistakes "the receiving side has obtained the object" for lifecycle completion, and also leaks device identification to the caller. It does not explain the meaning of empty bytes, does not provide a completion determination after import, and assumes that the caller should know how to wait.

There are two reasons not to delete it. First, it records why CPU private objects were initially prioritized: at the time, the platform layer had no confirmed unified action. Second, it remains a viable fallback direction. If the unified path ultimately can be sustained only by having callers read CPU private state, or if the waiting logic must be rewritten for each caller, we should not pretend that a general protocol already exists; we should fall back to explicit local adaptation and then redefine the interface boundaries.

The old path should not be misread as "CPU must always be specialized." It merely acknowledges that, when a general interface has not yet been established, a local implementation is more honest than a pretense of consistency.

## Actual objects near the file

The current starting point for verification is `lmcache/v1/platform/cpu/stub_cpu_device.py`. The following is visible at the top of the file:

```python
from __future__ import annotations
from contextlib import nullcontext
from typing import Any
from lmcache.logging import init_logger
```

These declarations provide local clues. `nullcontext` indicates that cases requiring no additional context entry can exist around the CPU path, but this does not mean "no synchronization is needed," much less determine on the caller's behalf when to confirm completion. `Any` allows the device adaptation layer to temporarily store opaque objects, but should not become a reason for upper layers to access private fields. Logging initialization only indicates that the file has a place to record logs; it does not indicate that any particular failure will automatically be converted into a completion state.

Therefore, this file is suitable for handling capability selection, event representation, and local waiting implementations on the CPU device side; it is not suitable for defining on its own how the cache directory applies placement changes, nor for providing callers with a dedicated protocol from here. The callers' actual reference relationships still need to be checked along the call sites, especially those that put importing and continued execution in the same branch.

## Two sets of disagreements left by the review meeting

One set of disagreements concerns the shape of the interface. Some favor dedicated methods for CPU export and import capabilities, on the grounds that the object form can be more direct; another view is to keep device differences within the implementation, with upper layers handling only unified lifecycle actions. "Unified" here is not understood as forcing all backends to use the same event data structure. What it requires is that callers be able to express the same kinds of intent: confirm support, hand off a transferable representation, restore it at the other end, obtain a completion determination, and synchronize when needed.

The other set of disagreements concerns where synchronization belongs. Embedding synchronization in import makes it simple for callers to use, but hides the cost of waiting and removes the choice from call sites that "only transfer, without waiting." Leaving synchronization entirely to callers makes call sites responsible again for interpreting the object's state after import. The current proposal does not choose between these two internal strategies on behalf of all call sites; it requires synchronization to be a callable lifecycle action, and completion state to be explicitly queryable both before and after synchronization.

The review comments also require the failure modes to be spelled out, rather than merely writing "CPU unavailable." At a minimum, distinguish among: the device does not support event IPC; it supports it, but the export contains no usable content; the receiving end cannot import it; completion cannot be determined after import; and the synchronization action cannot maintain the same interface boundary. These cases do not need to be handled identically. The first may indicate insufficient capability; the second through fourth indicate implementation or representation gaps; and the fifth indicates that the calling protocol still leaks device differences.

## Proposal After Narrowing the Trial Scope

This round does not put batched cache events, key-directory placement, the eviction controller, or token matching into the same trial. They may appear near the same business path, but the first objective of the IPC event is only to verify the lifecycle of a synchronization object after it is passed across endpoints. When the scope is too broad, any failure will simultaneously point to cache writing, event publication, directory updates, and device synchronization, making it impossible to determine the actual breakpoint.

The recommended path is as follows:

1. First confirm that the selected device path declares support for event IPC.
2. Generate an event and export its transferable representation.
3. Pass that representation to the receiving end for import.
4. Query the completion status of the imported object.
5. Request synchronization only when the call site actually needs to continue depending on the result at that point.

Between step 2 and step 3, empty content must not be interpreted as a valid event. Between step 3 and step 4, the return of the "import" function must not be interpreted as completion. Between step 4 and step 5, it is likewise not permitted to conceal whether the caller chose to wait. Each stopping point corresponds to a previously recorded misjudgment; the purpose is not to expand a limited trial into a comprehensive overhaul.

There are still two candidate implementation paths.

**Route A: CPU-specific surface.** CPU The device exposes its own export, import, and wait methods, and the caller invokes them according to the device type. This can be delivered quickly and also makes it convenient for CPU to use the simplest representation internally. The tradeoff is that the caller needs to know the device branches; once another backend has different naming or a different completion check, conditional branches will accumulate in the calling code.

**Route B: A device-agnostic surface.** The platform exposes a consistent set of lifecycle actions, and the CPU file provides one implementation. The cost is that completion checks and synchronization boundaries need to be clarified first, making it less direct than Route A in the short term. The benefit is that call sites do not need to interpret CPU private objects, and device differences can remain in the adapter layer.

For now, we will continue trying Route B, but will not elevate it into a conclusion that "all devices must have the same structure." CPU can still use its own representation, context management, and completion mechanism; the interface constrains only the actions and results callers need.

## Explicit revisions to earlier conclusions

An earlier statement was "having exported bytes is enough." This statement has been overturned. Bytes are not an isolated signal of success: they must be importable, and the imported object must be queryable as complete or incomplete.

Another earlier statement was "waiting can simply stay in the caller's existing logic." This statement no longer holds either. Call Fang Ke to choose whether to wait, but callers must not be forced to determine what to wait for through CPU private state. If synchronization requires callers to identify the device type and access private objects, the interface surface is not yet complete.

The final old assumption was "cache events and IPC event can share a single state object." This is not the current direction either. Cache events describe the information needed for cache writes and the directory; IPC event describes the transfer and completion of synchronization objects. The two can be adjacent within the same business action, but merging them would leave the receiver unable to tell whether it is dealing with cache placement information or synchronization state.

## Current interface contract

The backend-neutral event path must expose check_event_support, export_event, import_event, query_event, and synchronize_event as one CPU-capable lifecycle; exported bytes must be non-empty and the imported event must query as complete.

This convention constrains the calling surface; it does not specify the concrete type of event inside CPU. `check_event_support` distinguishes lack of support from a subsequent execution failure; `export_event` hands off a transferable representation; `import_event` restores a queryable object on the receiving side; `query_event` provides a completion check; `synchronize_event` is reserved for call sites that genuinely need to wait. These actions may be implemented by separate modules, as long as callers do not have to switch to a private CPU protocol.

The requirements for exported content also apply only to events that are exported. A business-logic branch with no event may end before entering the export step; once the export step is entered, the returned content must be sufficient for the receiving side to complete the import. This prevents empty content from being mistaken for a valid object on the receiving side, and prevents higher layers from treating "nothing to transfer" as a completed IPC transfer.

Querying completion after import is a point explicitly retained in this revision. It does not require the import to complete immediately, nor does it require every call site to synchronize; it requires callers to have an explicit way to know whether the current object is complete. If an implementation can provide status only after synchronization, that must also be clearly expressed through the interface behavior, rather than leaving callers to guess from exceptions, time intervals, or internal object fields.

## Notes on the Cache Event Bypass

CPU event IPC is not a replacement for the cache event publisher. When a cache write generates an event, `backend` in the published entry identifies the backend that generated that storage event; it is part of the cache event's metadata. A IPC event is a different kind of object, used to transfer synchronization state across boundaries.

This distinction is important for subsequent integration. If an L2 storage operation generates a cache event, the event entry should retain the corresponding `backend` so that consumers do not lose the storage source; however, this does not mean that the cache event itself already carries an importable, queryable IPC event. Conversely, the completion state of CPU event IPC does not replace the cache directory's handling of placement changes.

The trial does not specify an ordering between the two for now. A call site may complete the cache write before publishing the event, or it may need to wait on a synchronization object before proceeding. This ordering must be derived from the actual calling relationships; it cannot be inferred solely from adjacent declarations in the CPU adapter file. Only one thing is required here: do not merge the two kinds of objects into a single ambiguous state just because both appear near the cache path.

## Acceptance and Withdrawal

The minimum condition for accepting Route B is not "having all the method names," but that the same CPU path can perform support checking, non-empty export, import, completion querying, and synchronization on demand as a continuous sequence of actions. The caller does not read private fields of CPU, does not use the device type to determine what completion means, and does not mistakenly record a return from import as synchronization completion.

In the following cases, the current trial should be withdrawn and the discussion should return to localized adaptation:

- The exported representation can be empty, but there is no handling distinct from "no event";
- The receiver can import, but cannot obtain completion status;
- Synchronization can only be hidden in import side effects, leaving the call site unable to express whether to wait;
- The caller must branch on CPU to read an opaque object;
- Cached event metadata and IPC completion status are merged into the same object to preserve a unified surface.

Withdrawal does not mean removing CPU support. It merely acknowledges that the current interface is insufficient to support a device-independent lifecycle. At that point, the dedicated CPU implementation can remain, while the missing completion check or transfer representation is listed as a subsequent design issue.

## Adjacent issues not yet separated out

The interfaces for cache events and directory updates may still affect call ordering, but this proposal should not define directory semantics in advance. In particular, when metadata for cache writes is formed, when it is published, and when consumers can use it to update the placement index all belong to another protocol chain. Here, we only record its intersection with CPU IPC: both may appear in the same business operation, so implementers must not substitute the success of one object for the completion of another.

It also remains to be confirmed who ultimately provides event backend selection for the CPU file. If the device layer creates the implementation directly and the platform layer is only responsible for forwarding, ownership of the interface will be more concentrated at the CPU adaptation point; if the platform layer is responsible for selection, the CPU file should provide only capabilities and implementation entry points. The current material is insufficient to decide between these two organizational approaches.

Another unresolved item is where failures are logged. Log initialization already appears near the file, but this is not grounds for requiring all export or import failures to be logged in the same place. We first need to confirm which failures occur in the device adaptation layer and which occur on the caller side; otherwise, logging will conflate "unsupported," "empty representation," "import failure," and "incomplete" into one vague CPU issue.

## Appendix: Old examples

### Old example one: Verifying only object creation

The imagined path in the early experiment was: immediately treat a CPU event as transferable after creating it. This example is outdated because object creation did not cover exported content, receiver-side import, or completion querying. It is retained to remind subsequent reviews not to stop at the construction step.

### Old example two: completion upon return from import

Another old example calls the moment when the receiver obtains the object "IPC completion". This seems convenient when no completion query is available, but it cannot describe objects that have not yet completed, nor can it let call sites distinguish whether synchronization is needed. This example is no longer a basis for implementation.

### Old observations that remain reusable

The CPU path should keep device differences in the adaptation layer as much as possible; this has not changed. What has changed is the interpretation of "keeping them in the adaptation layer": it does not end with giving the caller a CPU private object, but instead allows the caller to express support, transfer, querying, and waiting through a stable lifecycle.

The next review should first trace the CPU call sites to identify the actual entry points for export and import, then determine which call site requests synchronization. If callers are found to already depend on private state, record that branch first; do not delete it outright when no replacement interface is available.

# Cache Event Send/Receive Troubleshooting Tree

The symptom is that the L2 cache shows evidence of a write, but the downstream receiver has no record that explains the processing outcome. Don't label this gap as a consumer failure yet; write completion, notification generation, notification receipt, and use of the received notification are four different things.

On call, first separate cases by the earliest break in the chain:

```text
Write present at cache location, no subsequent change
├─ No trace of a notification
│  └─ Stay near the write; don't investigate the receiver
├─ Trace of a notification, no receipt record
│  └─ Record the timing of the receiver's appearance
└─ Receipt record present, no change from processing
   └─ Keep the received contents; don't rush to resend
```

The original contract was simple: after the write completed, send an object-name hint, and let the receiver look up the rest of the contents itself. This was sufficient when there were few objects and processing was continuous, so old on-call pages often recorded only the object name. It also made it easy to conflate "a notification was sent" with "the notification was sufficient to use."

The old issue name leads to `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/connector/mooncakestore_connector.py`. Keep that as a starting point for tracing back; it does not mean the connector owns the entire send/receive path. If the notification appeared but the receiver appeared only afterward, record it as a timing issue; don't resend and overwrite the evidence of whether the first notification arrived. If there is already evidence at the receiver but the result is unchanged, save the object contents received at the time and the batch boundaries for review by someone who can confirm the consumption rules.

# Cache Event Send/Receive Troubleshooting Tree

This page still starts with a narrow observation: the cache location has been written to, but the receiving side lacks enough information to explain the subsequent actions. Last year's tree remains, but "sending a notification is enough" can no longer be a stopping condition. The same outward symptom has at least three possible sources: no notification was created after the write, a notification was created but the receiver was not present, or the receiver got the content but lacked the context needed to act on it.

```text
No change on the consumer side after the L2 cache write completes
│
├─ No evidence of an event
│  ├─ Only the write has been confirmed
│  │  └─ Stop at the write side; do not record this as a receive failure
│  └─ The order of the write and notification is unclear
│     └─ Keep the original record; do not fill in the sequence
│
├─ Evidence of an event, but no trace at the receiving end
│  ├─ The receiving end appeared after the event
│  │  └─ Record as registration timing; do not resend yet
│  └─ The receiving end was already present
│     └─ Check whether registration and sending occurred in the same processing cycle
│
└─ A trace exists at the receiving end, but the result has not changed
   ├─ The received content is too short
   │  └─ Return to the write side and save the original content
   └─ The same object appears again
      └─ Record as a duplicate candidate first, not as successful recovery
```

## Retained Previous Guidance

The original margin note from 2023 reads: "The object name is enough; the receiving end can look up the other fields itself." This explains why the old records started the investigation on the consumer side. At the time, the assumption was that every receiving end could return to the same storage view, so the object name seemed sufficient to connect the subsequent processing steps.

This passage is no longer suitable as an operational action, but it stays in the document. In one review, the receiving end saw the object name but still could not determine which write it was dealing with; classifying this as "the receiver was late" did not solve the problem. An object name only shows that an object was mentioned, not that the rest of the event context can be filled in.

The old page also said, "If the receiving end has no record, resend once." That is no longer the default action either. Resending changes the two facts most in need of preservation: whether the first notification had already arrived, and whether the same object appearing later was being processed for the first time or being seen again. Temporary recovery may have its own procedure, but an investigation record cannot substitute a resend for observation.

## Review Entry Points

Connectors are still a common place to look back for old issue names and call names:

```python
from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional, no_type_check
import asyncio
import json
import os
```

These lines do not say who owns sending or consumption. They only remind the on-call engineer to keep three judgments separate: whether the asynchronous timing is known, whether the content is still in container form, and whether the content has been serialized. "No change at the receiving end" does not justify choosing any one of these as the cause.

One approach failed during review: attributing every unchanged result to late receiver registration and having the receiving end wait for the next notification. This did not answer whether the first notification was complete, or whether the second would obscure the duplicate path. The conclusion retained afterward was narrow: registration timing is a separate branch and cannot replace an assessment of the content.

Another common leap is to ask the receiving side to read back by object name when the event content is short. This assumes the receiving side always has the same storage context; this page has no evidence to support that assumption. When content is insufficient, first save what is available, then return to the end that produced the notification; do not make the receiving end guess the source first.

## On-Call Branches

**No evidence of a notification after the write**: Record the write trace and whether a subsequent notification action can be confirmed. If only a change at the cache location can be confirmed, stop at the producing side. Do not rewrite this as a consumer failure just because the consumer side is empty.

**Evidence of a notification, but no receive record**: First check whether the receiving end appeared before or after the notification. If it appeared late, preserve that ordering; do not require it to catch up on past content. Only if the receiving end appeared first and there is still no trace should you check whether the registration entry point and the send entry point refer to the same processing cycle.

**A record at the receiving end, but no change**: First retain the received content and the boundaries of that batch. Do not collapse the object name, source clues, and size clues into "content received." If you cannot determine whether the content is sufficient, do not turn to modifying the receiving end.

**The same object appears again**: Write "duplicate candidate." Without the previous batch's boundaries, you cannot assert that this is a replay or a new write. The old page recommended running the consumption flow again for any duplicate; that recommendation is no longer used because it would make the subsequent state unable to distinguish between the first and second processing attempts.

## Review Addendum

The review only asked for clear stopping points: with no notification, stop at the producing side; when the receiving end appears late, stop at timing; when content is insufficient, stop at event construction; when an object appears again, stop at determining whether it has already been processed. These stopping points are not meant to add steps, but to avoid collapsing different situations into "subscription anomaly."

One adjacent question has not yet been split out: when the same object appears in different write batches, should it be treated as the same event? This page only requires retaining batch boundaries; it does not settle the cross-batch judgment.

# Cache Event Send/Receive Troubleshooting Tree

When a cache location already shows a write but the subsequent state does not change, the incident often comes down to a single statement: "the consumer side did not move." That statement is not enough to point to either end. It could mean that no event was formed after the write, that the event was formed but not delivered to any receiver, or that the receiver already encountered the content but did not enter its own subsequent processing boundary.

The on-duty record should first note the earliest break point that can be confirmed. Do not infer what happened the first time from a later resend, re-registration, or state change.

```text
The cache location shows a write, but the subsequent state is unchanged
│
├─ The event did not appear
│  ├─ No creation or delivery clues after the write
│  │  └─ Stop at the producer side; the blank receiver side is not part of the determination
│  └─ Only know that the object existed later
│     └─ Write "event path unconfirmed"
│
├─ The event appeared, but the receiver side has no trace
│  ├─ The receiver side appeared after the event
│  │  └─ Record the order; do not use a resend in place of a record
│  ├─ The receiver side appeared first
│  │  └─ Check whether registration and sending entered the same processing cycle
│  └─ The time when the receiver side appeared is unknown
│     └─ Stop at the sequencing determination; do not classify it as missing content
│
└─ The receiver side has a trace, but the processing result is unchanged
   ├─ The content is insufficient to identify the source or object scope
   │  └─ Return to the producer side and preserve the original content received
   ├─ This batch's content may have appeared before
   │  └─ Write "duplicate candidate"; do not process it again as a new batch
   └─ Both the content and the timing have been recorded
      └─ Then check the receiver side's own processing boundary
```

This tree has never been consolidated into a new guide. Some actions in the old records are no longer recommended, but old tickets and handoff text still use their wording; deleting them instead would make it unclear why the wrong place was checked first at the time. What follows preserves the layers left by several additions, and not all sections use the current policy.

## 2023: Rules initially written on the duty page

The earliest entry point was `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/connector/mooncakestore_connector.py`. Exception names and call names often led people toward the connector, so it was recorded as "the file to open first." This is only a lookup location, not a determination of ownership for the entire send/receive path.

At the time, the working rules were only two sentences: issue a notification as soon as possible after a secondary-cache write; the receiver side should look up the remaining information by object name. The troubleshooting tree was also very short then:

```text
There is a write, but no subsequent change
├─ The receiver side has no record: make the receiver side appear again
└─ The receiver side has a record: send the notification once more
```

This old tree remains here because historical records will refer to the words "make the receiver side appear again." Its flaw is also straightforward: it compressed writing, sending, registration, and processing into one continuous action. The content seen after the receiver side reappears cannot prove that it was already available when the first notification appeared; sending again also cannot show whether the first notification arrived.

It was also assumed at the time that the object name was sufficient. This assumption worked for tying together a very small incident, but it did not explain where the receiver side should retrieve the content from, nor did it require preserving the source and object size. The old page's "matching object names are enough to reuse the previous determination" later became one source of misjudgment, but it reflects the actual practice of that version, so it is not rewritten as a rule that did not exist at the time.

## A Note Left in the Margin

An early on-call margin note said: "Without a receiver, the consumer usually hasn't started." It was not fully reviewed and was not treated as an official conclusion. It conflated at least three states into one: the receiving end does not exist at all, the receiving end was registered only after the event, or the receiving end already existed but did not enter the same processing path.

These three states require different evidence. When the receiving end does not exist, all we can say is that there was no available entry point at that moment; when the receiving end appears late, we should record which event it appeared after; only when the receiving end appeared first but left no trace is it worth continuing to investigate the relationship between registration and sending. If all we have on site is "the consumer side did nothing," none of the above can yet be established.

Another sentence once left in the margin was: "Resending can get a stuck notification through." This may be useful as a temporary mitigation, but it does not belong at the front of the decision tree. Resending is not an observation step. It overwrites questions that need to be preserved first: whether the initial notification existed, whether the initial notification was complete, and whether the same batch of content had already been processed.

## 2024: Limitations Observed Near the Connector

The review did not turn the connector into the protocol's sole entry point. The direct dependencies visible in the file header are as follows:

```python
from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional, no_type_check
import asyncio
import json
import os
```

This content supports only a very limited reminder: asynchronous ordering, fields in the container, and serialized content should not be conflated as the same type of anomaly. It does not tell us who the sender is, nor how the consumer should apply it. Therefore, the wording in the old record—"look at the connector first, then assess the entire chain"—needs to be downgraded to a navigation habit rather than a diagnostic conclusion.

That review once attempted to uniformly classify "no change" as a late registration: if no record of the receiving end was found, wait for the next notification. This attempt was not adopted later. Waiting for the next one cannot answer whether the first notification contained anything at all; if the next content is different, the original evidence will be overwritten; if the content is the same, the final state still cannot tell us whether the change occurred only on the second attempt or whether the first was already processed and the second ignored.

The rule added afterward is not "a late registration is always harmless"; it is to treat registration timing separately. First record the order in which the event and the receiving end each appeared, then examine the content. Insufficient content and late registration can occur at the same time; neither can be used to erase the other.

One other old habit was retained but marked as outdated: when event content is brief, require the receiving side to read it back by object name. This action assumes that all receiving sides can access the same storage context. This page contains no evidence supporting that assumption. When the receiving end receives insufficient content, first save the portion already received, then return to the producing end to determine whether anything was omitted during construction; do not make the receiving end guess the source.

## Processing Order That Was Not Adopted

The following passage was once posted as a temporary recommendation next to the old link and is now deprecated:

```text
1. Have the receiving end register again;
2. Resend the notification;
3. As long as a subsequent state changes, record it as recovered.
```
The problem is not that the three steps can never be performed, but that they were written as the basis for determining facts. Re-registering at the receiving end can only change the subsequent existence state; resending can only add one new delivery opportunity; and state changes may also result from the first, second, or some other adjacent action. When a historical ticket uses this wording, first return to the first breakpoint at the beginning of this page rather than executing the steps in their original order.

The example that "the object names are the same, so this is the same processing" is equally outdated. The same object may mean that the same object appeared again, or it may simply mean that different batches reference the same object. Without a batch boundary, it can only be written as a duplicate candidate. An object name alone cannot prove that the source is the same, the size is the same, or that the previous occurrence was already processed.

## 2024 On-site entry format after review

The review did not require a complete report for every anomaly; it only required that the record not go past the first blank. When filling it out, leave the following information in this order:

1. Whether a write trace exists at the cache location;
2. Whether it can be confirmed that an event was formed after the write;
3. Whether the receiving end appeared before or after the event;
4. Whether the receiving end left a trace of receipt;
5. Whether the received content can still distinguish the object scope, source, and size;
6. Whether the current batch may already have appeared earlier.

If 2 has no answer, the following items can be left blank. Do not fill 2 in as "send failed" just because the receiving end happens to be empty. When 3 indicates that the receiving end appeared later, you can still record the content received afterward, but you cannot treat the later state as evidence that it was either not received or received the first time.

When multiple receiving ends exist, do not merge them into "consumer started." Clearly record, one by one, who has a receipt trace, who does not, and who appeared later. A follow-up action at one receiving end cannot explain another receiving end's blank; a receiving end that appeared later cannot explain the reason for one that appeared earlier.

## 2025 Supplemental navigation and rollback records

Later, RCP-203 became navigation entry points for this type of anomaly boundary. The card has shown, at different times, statuses for rollback checks and restarting processing; these statuses only indicate that the work item was viewed or reopened, and cannot replace this page's judgment about the event breakpoint. When work needs to be linked, it can be accessed through RCP-203; do not copy the card's status text as a conclusion about the send/receive protocol.

This phase clearly separates two distinctions that are often confused: generating a notification and registering a recipient are two points in time; whether an event arrives and whether it contains enough information for the receiving side to process it are two content-related judgments. Both can go wrong together, or only one may go wrong. When the records show both "the receiving endpoint appeared late" and "insufficient content," there is no need to force a single root cause.

Someone also suggested consolidating all anomalies into the connector file. This suggestion was not retained. The connector remains a nearby location that the old issue name can point to, but if the first breakpoint observed on site is already on the receiving side, the investigation should not circle back just to follow the old path. The imports at the top of the file can only indicate local connections to asynchronous operations, containers, and serialization; they cannot define the responsibility boundaries of the entire protocol.

## Corrections Following the Review Excerpts

The review required moving "resending" from a default step to exception handling. The reason is not that resending necessarily causes problems, but that it changes the two facts most worth preserving: whether the first event arrived, and whether the same batch of content has already been processed. Without these two judgments, any subsequent success is insufficient to show where in the sequence the original problem occurred.

Another change that the review required making explicit was: when the receiving endpoint is empty, "there is no recipient" and "no event was received" must not be written as the same statement. The former is a registration or existence state; the latter is a delivery state. When the two are written together, people following up can easily end up checking the wrong side.

The review did not require this page to specify directory updates, eviction policies, or caller recovery. These items may affect the final state, but they are not the first breakpoint in the send/receive protocol. They remain adjacent issues and are not included in the current troubleshooting tree.

## Protocol Boundaries in the Current Record

Starting with this version, at least the clues about the source, objects, and sizes of the same batch of content must be preserved between the producing side and the receiving side; the receiving endpoint's registration and the isolation of its own processing must also be recorded separately. To prevent the old page from splitting these items apart again, the current cross-check uses the following wording: The cache event protocol is built around CacheEventSink, CacheEventSubscriber, and CacheEventBroadcaster: L2_KEYS_STORED enters through _on_l2_store, preserves backend, keys, and sizes metadata, and fan-out uses register_consumer plus the consumer-side fence_instance hook.

This guidance changes two old assumptions. First, notifications are no longer just object-name hints. The content created on the producer side must preserve the correspondence among `backend`, `keys`, and `sizes`; when there is more than one object, do not keep only an aggregate size, and do not separate sizes from object records. Second, whether a receiver enters fan-out through `register_consumer` and whether the receiver's own `fence_instance` participates in the subsequent boundary are not the same question.

When investigating the producer side, confirming that a secondary-storage event exists does not mean confirming that the receiver can process it. First check whether `L2_KEYS_STORED` forms content via `_on_l2_store`; if the content is available in the environment being investigated, record the source backend, object keys, and corresponding sizes. The stopping point here is "whether event construction leaves enough content," not "whether the consumer can reconstruct all the information by guessing."

When investigating fan-out, first ask whether the receiver is already in the path for this round through `register_consumer`. A receiver that does not exist, one that registered late, and one that registered but has no evidence of receipt remain different branches. Only after there is evidence that the receiver has received the event should you check whether it reaches the processing boundary where `fence_instance` resides. Missing registration manifests as not participating in fan-out; a processing boundary that has not occurred may instead manifest as receipt with no state change. Do not call both subscription failures.

The following are several stopping points that can be used directly in the current tree:

**A write is visible, but no event content is visible.** Preserve the material surrounding the write, mark the event path as unconfirmed, and stop at the producer side. Do not have the receiver register again as a substitute for this determination.

**Event content is visible, but the receiver appeared late.** Record which event occurred before the receiver appeared. Processing that occurs afterward can be recorded as a subsequent observation, but must not be used to infer the delivery status of the first event retroactively.

**The receiver appeared first, but there is no evidence of receipt.** Check whether registration and sending entered the same processing round. If the two sides cannot be matched, preserve the timing sequence and stop; do not classify this directly as insufficient content.

**The receiver has received the event, but the content is missing some of the clues in `backend`, `keys`, or `sizes`.** Return to the producer side and preserve the original content. Do not follow the old rule of having the receiver read the data back on its own, and do not use the presence of an object name to prove that the content is complete.

**The receiver has received the event, and the content is complete, but processing remains unchanged.** Then determine whether the current batch has appeared before. If the previous batch's boundary is incomplete, record it only as a duplicate candidate; do not record the second observation directly as a new write.

## Adjacent issues not yet separated out

This page does not define what conditions are sufficient to prove that repeated appearances of the same object across multiple batches represent the same write. The current requirement is only to preserve batch boundaries and stop at a duplicate candidate when no determination can be made. Neither the same source backend nor the same object name is sufficient on its own to resolve this issue.

Another open item is whether a relatively long gap between the write trace and event arrival should be listed separately as an on-call signal. An older page used to label every gap as receiver-side latency, but that was later corrected; now the gap is recorded only as a time phenomenon. Without supporting material, do not assign it to a responsible endpoint.

If the incident ultimately lands in coordination-side batch-processing encapsulation, rather than the send/receive boundary covered by this page, see DOC-17 instead. That page handles another set of objects; do not bring its migration steps into the current tree.

## Appendix: Two phrasings that still appear in historical records

**Old example 1:** "Make the receiving end reappear first, then resend the notification; if the status changes, processing is complete." This wording is deprecated. It erases the distinctions among the initial event, registration order, and duplicate processing. When encountering this wording, restart the assessment from whether an event clue exists after the cache write.

**Old example 2:** "The object names match, so the previous result can be reused." This wording is also no longer applicable. Matching object names may simply mean that the same object has appeared again; they cannot prove that the source, size, batch boundaries, or prior processing status are the same.

One brief note still applies: if all that remains at the incident site is the result at the cache location, with no material showing event construction, receipt registration, or received content, stop the record at "Unable to confirm the event path after the write." Do not fill this gap in as a definite failure of the connector, receiving end, or directory.

# ObjectKey Wire-Format History

This page started with a narrowly scoped interface review: test file `tests/v1/distributed/test_encoded_object_key.py` was used to revisit the wire format of ObjectKey, with the discussion focused on whether the fields could still be reconstructed from wire values and whether `cache_salt` was caller input or an encoder constraint. The record did not extend to the distributed-cache read/write flow.

## Options Compared at the Time

Two approaches remained on the table. The first retained `ObjectKey` as the field model and treated `EncodedObjectKey` as a thin wrapper between testing and transport. The second treated the encoded string as the sole object, with callers storing only that string and no longer distinguishing `model`, `name`, `rank`, `group`, `salt`, and the chunk hash. The latter required fewer changes, but once something went wrong, only the full text string could be compared; there was no way to tell which segment caused the difference.

The decision at the time was to retain two object layers: `ObjectKey` for expressing the fields and `EncodedObjectKey` for the wire representation. The reason was not to pursue shorter strings, but to keep field-level differences visible during investigation. The test file's adjacent import reflected the same decision:

```python
from dataclasses import asdict
import pytest
from lmcache.v1.distributed.api import EncodedObjectKey, ObjectKey
```

This import was the boundary that could be confirmed at the time. It shows that the test references both objects and the field-expansion utility; file location alone cannot establish that the encoding implementation belongs to the test directory, nor can the test file be treated as a production entry point.

## Old Judgment Retained

The old record took a permissive view of delimiters. It treated `cache_salt` as a fragment already prepared by the caller, and held that as long as the final string could be read back by the same code, special characters did not need to be rejected during object construction. This judgment was not removed in the meeting, and later verification did not rewrite this section, so this page cannot serve as current input-validation guidance.

An adjacent counterexample exposed the gap in that position exactly: when `cache_salt` contains a delimiter that creates ambiguity, external behavior throws `ValueError`. The old conclusion still treated this as a "caller guarantee," but the counterexample had already shifted the responsibility boundary toward the encoding entry point; both passages coexist in this old material. When determining a specific version, first check whether the caller passes salt as free text; do not quote only the line saying "can be read back."

## Wire-Format Sample

The hash notes also did not adopt the idea that only hexadecimal length matters. The test sample expands the raw chunk hash into lowercase hexadecimal text; in the sample, `chunk_hash_hex` is `736861726564`. The value retained here is the one seen on the wire, not a separately created binary object; when investigating, compare it item by item with the object after field expansion.

No new protocol table listing the order of all fields was written at the time; the only decision was to continue using the existing objects and test entry point to observe differences. Accordingly, the actions supported by this decision are limited: confirm that the input is still represented by `ObjectKey`, confirm that the encoding result includes the corresponding hash text, and then check whether a salt containing a delimiter triggers the exception above. It cannot prove that other cache events, directory indexes, or callers already follow the same constraints.

## Revisit Entry Point

To revisit this decision, first open `tests/v1/distributed/test_encoded_object_key.py`, starting at the locations where `ObjectKey`, `EncodedObjectKey`, and `chunk_hash_hex` occur. The file header's `asdict` and `pytest` provide only clues about field expansion and assertions. Implementation ownership, the production call chain, and actual values in the old cache are left to their respective materials; this page retains only the options, counterexample, and old interpretation left by this review of ObjectKey wire invariants.

The review later filed it under Quality and Regression materials, but did not produce a new complete decision. If this page is cited, the historical choice to retain two object layers is fair to cite; citing "delimiters are the caller's responsibility" must be read together with `ValueError`—the counterexample.

versions.body:
# Webhook Injection Compatibility Plan

This draft retains the original approach of handling the two issues side by side: the webhook injection of CacheBlend and the namespace-qualified engine references may appear around the same invocation, but they are not determined by the same interface. The earlier draft described "fill in the inputs first, then try" very broadly, and the later review did not change that wording into a compatibility commitment. What is added here is how far a trial can be meaningfully discussed, which records can allow the next review to continue, and which observations can only bring the trial to a stop.

The early trade-offs are still useful. Checking only injection without touching the reference form can narrow the scope of a single attempt; directly accepting qualified references can expose naming issues introduced by the caller sooner; changing both can approach a complete invocation, but loses the ability to localize differences. The second or the first option was not chosen at the time, not because they were considered infeasible, but because there was no concrete input explaining at what boundary "acceptance" occurs. That was the working position at the time and should not be treated as the current interface conclusion.

The third direction left open initially was not meant to be deferred indefinitely either. It requires first identifying a recognizable entry point, then ensuring that the input, result, and changes come from the same execution. Without this constraint, any resulting Pod shape could merely be an artifact of some undocumented condition. The draft did not attribute this uncertainty to the webhook or to the engine references; it simply refused to let a result lacking input decide for both sides.

The navigation back to the code side is `operator/internal/webhook/pod_injector_test.go`. The file is under `package webhook`, and its header begins the dependency declarations with `import (`. It is an adjacent entry point for injection-related tests and is suitable for finding or placing checks connected to Pod injection; this path alone cannot determine whether engine references should be interpreted by the webhook, the caller, or another layer. The earlier investigation also traced the issue name and call name back to this file, so this page has consistently described it as a review entry point rather than evidence of implementation ownership.

This distinction affects how trials are recorded. If a work item only confirms that an injection scenario exists near the test file, that does not mean it has confirmed that qualified references are resolved on the injection side. Conversely, the fact that a caller can complete an operation with a qualified name does not mean that the Pod mutation meets expectations. The two pieces of evidence can appear in the same review, but the conclusions must still be written separately.

## Trial boundaries on the injection side

CacheBlend webhook injection compatibility focuses on whether the injection process leaves any unexpected Pod changes after a corresponding invocation. The entry retained later by RCP-207 requires the corresponding operation to be run in a clean working directory, with the exit code, file changes, and residual directories checked. The clean directory here is only the starting point for comparison: it gives the file changes and residual content left by one execution a recognizable before-and-after relationship; it does not add new product semantics to the webhook.

The minimum record on the injection side should first clearly state the input, then retain the exit code, and afterward record the file changes and residual directories. Without the input, the generated artifacts cannot show which injection condition took effect; if the exit code is not as expected, the subsequent directory state cannot be written up as proof of compatibility either. If the file changes and residual directories cannot be tied to the same execution, they likewise cannot be combined into a conclusion that "injection succeeded."

In the earlier discussion, some people preferred to inspect the generated Pod first and then fill in the command parameters. That order did not help with the issue at the time. A Pod shape can result from multiple unrecorded conditions, while injection compatibility requires knowing exactly where the current action began. The trial can stop first at "what input was received, what did the execution return, and what did the directory retain," without prematurely characterizing every Pod difference.

RCP-207 Later assignment records shifted the focus to Operator webhook and payload lifecycle. This change shows that the two work items were adjacent in scheduling, but it is not a reason to conclude that they share an interface. This page does not fold the payload lifecycle assessment into webhook injection compatibility, nor does it use an assignment change to replace the injection-side input record. Exception handling related to payload staging remains within the scope of DOC-21.

## Trial boundaries on the reference side

The issue with namespace-qualified engine references first requires retaining the reference form actually written by the caller, and then confirming what the user can still see after the command completes. There is no need to organize all output into a table; what needs to be retained is a result sufficient to determine whether that reference remains visible. If the reference form was not recorded, then even if someone later sees a completed status, it is impossible to determine whether what they saw was the same qualified form.

The follow-up work in RCP-213 started from the notation in the help text and required confirmation of what the user could still see after the operation completed. The later review retained only an unedited pytest node transcript and environment details. This shows that the reference side was still being verified, and that someone at the time preserved the original state around the inputs and outputs; it is not enough to infer that some namespace-qualified engine references had been accepted by the webhook, nor can it replace a decision about the boundary of reference interpretation.

The reference side can be stopped independently. If the run only confirms that the command ended but cannot clearly state the reference result visible to the user, it should not be recorded as compatible. If the reference form and the transcript came from different conditions, retain them separately rather than combining them into one successful trial. The resulting material may be incomplete, but it is more suitable for the next review than piecing together unrelated fragments into a conclusion afterward.

## No longer treating the two paths as one check

The earlier draft used "one trial" to summarize the two objects, which could easily make people think that every run had to cover both at the same time. In practice, the two sides should be allowed to prepare separately: the injection side first confirms the directory, exit code, and file changes; the reference side first saves the actual form, the result visible to the user, and any necessary node transcript. Only when both sides have comparable material is there a reason to observe them around the same input.

Joint observation can still be a candidate, but it is not the current decision. Its value is that it comes close to one caller operation; the cost is that any difference could come from webhook mutation, the reference form, or the environment at the time. Once a joint result shows a difference while the corresponding separate material is not yet ready, the joint explanation can only be withdrawn; the issue cannot be attributed to either object.

The candidate options currently retained are as follows:

- **Separate trial**: For CacheBlend webhook injection compatibility, record only the changes after injection; for namespace-qualified engine references, record only the visible reference result. This makes the two results easier to distinguish, but cannot explain in one run what happens when they appear together.
- **Joint trial**: Use the same input to trigger injection and the qualified reference at the same time, while retaining the directory changes and node transcript. This approaches one caller operation, but any difference must be explained by returning to separate samples.
- **Continue deferring**: Do not enter implementation; only supplement the minimum input and expected output. This will not write unconfirmed behavior into the interface, but it will leave the caller facing two unresolved points.

The first version leaned toward continuing to defer, based on a gap in the evidence rather than a rejection of the functionality. The separate trial is not being written as a formal decision now either: it simply separates the uncertainty more clearly than the earlier draft. The joint trial has not been rejected, but before separate material appears, a compatibility judgment should not be proposed based on a single mixed result.

The withdrawal conditions need to be more specific than "roll back if the result is wrong." If a trial cannot list the inputs, cannot retain the exit code, or cannot tie the directory changes and residual directories to the same execution, return to deferred status. On the reference side, if all that is known is that the command ended but it is not possible to identify the reference result still visible to the user, do not record it as compatible. If a joint trial shows a difference while the separate sample is missing, withdraw the explanation of the difference's source; do not roll back an implementation that has not yet occurred.

Subsequent records added two verification entry points to this draft without closing either side. RCP-207 remain suitable for continuing to check the directory, exit code, and change records for CacheBlend webhook injection compatibility; RCP-213 remain suitable for continuing to check the actual form and user-visible result of namespace-qualified engine references. The two cards appear here to preserve where the work went at the time, not to indicate that they have already provided the same answer.

The undecided issues have not been reduced to a slogan: whether the injection side should be responsible for interpreting qualified references; which Pod changes before and after injection are expected; and whether a joint trial will still be worthwhile once the separate samples are ready. The first two still lack concrete input, and the last depends on whether the first two can leave comparable records.

This page continues to be referenced because it preserves why the work did not enter implementation at the time and preserves the two verification entry points, not because it has already defined the current compatibility rules.
