# Caller Integration Testing Exit Window Procedure

The exit window for lmcache-client-integration does not handle release approval. It only records three facts side by side: what exit action the caller took, the last result observed after that action, and whether any integration feedback still needs to be handed over to the next maintainer. The relevant maintainer signs off separately on whether the release succeeded.

Before the window starts, determine where this round's records pick up. The entry point used here is `docs/adj-lmcache/release/lmcache-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`; if the person taking over arrives from a daily report, an old link, or another documentation page, first return to this entry point to check the current integration testing records. The same entry point name does not mean the records belong to the same round, especially since there has already been a case where the entry point guidance was not updated when the expiration action occurred.

## Window-Opening Records

- [ ] Mark the scope of callers for this round in the integration testing records. The scope covers only callers that have already participated in lmcache-client-integration, not candidates that have yet to integrate.
- [ ] Record the entry point used at the start of this round. If the entry point changes later, record the change point near the original location rather than overwriting the old entry point with the new one.
- [ ] Write down the original input that can be used for comparison and the first result observed. The result here is the response, status, or integration feedback actually seen by the caller; if it was not seen, write not obtained rather than filling it in with conjecture.
- [ ] Check whether `token window` is already open. Its purpose is to define the observation scope for this round of checks, not to signal that records may be deleted early.
- [ ] If this round depends on a temporary entry point, a bypass, or additional permissions, note that it is still in use. Before exiting, do not remove it just because the main path is working normally.

This section does not require a new integration testing master table. RCPA-008 once proposed maintaining a separate exit entry point and timeline, but that was later canceled, and the relevant information went back to being maintained at the existing registration entry point. Window records should stay with the existing entry point; when daily reports or other pages need to mention them, just include a link.

## Review the Last Result

Keep one observed result from before the exit action and one from after it; there is no need to copy every attempt into the checklist. At a minimum, the records must let the person taking over see which caller the result came from, whether it was obtained before or after the exit action, and whether it was affected by an entry point change.

- [ ] If the result comes from the normal integration testing path, keep it together with this round's input and caller feedback.
- [ ] If the setup was temporarily changed for diagnosis, label this result separately as a post-diagnostic result. A difference between it and the pre-change result cannot be calculated directly, and it cannot replace the original setup.
- [ ] If the entry point changes during the window, clearly separate the periods before and after the change. RCPA-009 recorded that statistics from before and after an entry point change cannot be compared directly; without a change point, do not make trend judgments.
- [ ] If only a secondhand report is available and the actual result has not been seen, retain the scope of that report and leave the status unconfirmed, without checking off the result as verified.
- [ ] If the caller provides feedback about rejection or integration failure, keep that feedback in this round's records. Do not delete it just because it is not a successful result.

"Last" means only the last result that could be confirmed before this window closes, not that the system will produce no new results afterward. When observation continues in the next round, start a separate record rather than appending a seemingly continuous tail to this round.

## Perform the Exit Actions

Exit should begin with actions that the caller can still review. First confirm that the target of the exit actually belongs to this round of lmcache-client-integration, then perform cleanup; do not remove integration records with similar names along with it.

1. [ ] Verify the exit actions the caller has already performed. If an action has left no record that can be reviewed, mark it as pending confirmation, not "notified".
2. [ ] Check the caller's result once more after the action, and record that result immediately next to the action. If there is no result, retain the fact that there is no result.
3. [ ] Check `consumer fan-out`. The main call ending does not mean related calls have stopped; callers still waiting for results need to remain within the window.
4. [ ] Only after confirming that related calls no longer use the temporary entry point should you revoke the bypass, temporary permissions, or anything else retained solely for integration testing.
5. [ ] If a cleanup task would change the setup still being observed, stop first. First record that the action has not yet been performed and why, rather than changing the sample just to complete the checklist.

Do not represent "cleanup complete" as a single checkbox here. The exit action, the completion of related calls, and the removal of temporary entry points may happen at different times. Record each result separately so the person taking over can tell whether the window is blocked on the caller, the entry point, or feedback that is not yet complete.

## webhook Branch

`webhook mutation` is the explicit stop point on this page. If it has not appeared, do not infer from other normal signals that exit is complete.

- [ ] If it has appeared, record which caller result it appeared near, then continue checking related calls and temporary entry points.
- [ ] If it has not appeared, stop closing the window and do not remove an integration testing entry point that this branch might still use.
- [ ] If it has appeared but cannot be matched to this round's callers, keep the record without treating it as a pass for this round.
- [ ] If only the main path has a result and this branch has none, the main path result can be retained as the last visible result, but the window's status is still incomplete.

Earlier records described the action to take when this signal was absent too briefly, making it easy to read as "check again later". This has been changed to an explicit stop because subsequent cleanup could deprive the person taking over of the conditions needed to continue verifying this branch.

## Writing the Handoff

The supplementary record requirements in RCPA-007 are the person handing over, the person taking over, and the confirmation time. For an exit window, at a minimum, record who is handing over, who is receiving, and the recipient's confirmation of which part of the records they received. The handoff does not need to repeat the entire integration testing history; include only the specific actions still unfinished, the location of the last visible result, and the reason for stopping.

- [ ] If someone is taking over, specify whether they are taking over entry point verification, caller feedback, related calls, or recovery actions.
- [ ] If there is a confirmation time, put it next to the handoff item; if the time is blank, the window cannot be marked as handed over.
- [ ] Even when handing over to the same maintainer to continue the work, retain a handoff item. This prevents unfinished actions from being disguised as unclaimed old records.
- [ ] If there is only an on-duty handoff and no exit entry point verification, still treat it as incomplete. Previous records have already shown that things matching up for the person on duty in that round does not mean the exit entry point has been tried.

There are still no results for recovery actions in the shared environment. Do not write "recovery available" in place of "recovery not triggered", and do not check off this item along with the exit action just because that action worked normally. If recovery records are obtained later, separately state which caller and window they correspond to, rather than backfilling them as results that had already been verified at the time of this round.

## Sequence Before Closing the Window

When closing the window, follow the actual dependencies, not the number of checked boxes on the page: first confirm the last visible result, then confirm the exit action, then check `consumer fan-out` and `webhook mutation`, and finally handle temporary entry points and the handoff. If there is no evidence for an earlier action, subsequent cleanup can be paused.

- [ ] This round's entry point and its change points have been retained.
- [ ] The caller's exit actions are recorded.
- [ ] The last visible result after the action has been retained, or it is explicitly stated that no result was obtained.
- [ ] Related calls that are still waiting have been marked.
- [ ] `webhook mutation` has appeared and can be matched to this round, or the window has explicitly stopped at this item.
- [ ] Temporary entry points, bypasses, and permissions are removed only after confirming that they are no longer serving calls.
- [ ] Unfinished items have a person taking over and a confirmation time.

Any missing item can stop the window from closing. When stopping, retain the current entry point, the exit actions already performed, and the last visible result; do not fabricate judgments to make the records look tidy. If the entry point has changed, the expiration action is no longer valid, or the statistics are not comparable, do not go back and rewrite the original records of an old window either.

RCPA-009 are used to review the statistical boundary caused by entry point changes; RCPA-007 are used to supplement handoff information; RCPA-008 preserve the background on why a separate exit timeline is no longer being created. They are all supporting entry points for the current checklist, not substitutes for the records here of this round's exit actions and stop points.

# Unadopted integration approach

Two approaches were on the table during integration testing: continue using `cache-event batch`, or split `eviction pin` out on its own. This note records the latter without treating it as the agreed integration approach.

The preference at the time was to split it out because the two sections in `docs/adj-lmcache/proposals/rejected-lmcache-client-integration-approach.md` had different failure exit paths. # Unadopted Integration Route Proposal

This route was ultimately not retained as the integration method for lmcache-client-integration. This draft is still kept because the reasons for opposing it at the time were not limited to "larger changes": the comparison targets, the callers that had not been found, and what needed to be restored on rollback were discussed in the same round. Later ticket review also did not produce enough material to rewrite the old assessment as a current conclusion.

The original wording reduced the choice to two options: one would continue along `cache-event batch`, and the other would take `eviction pin` out of the batch path. This wording itself had limitations. It only described the two destinations seen in the integration draft; it did not establish that they covered all callers, nor did it say which entry point would be switched first if the option were actually adopted.

## Why splitting was considered at the time

The old draft noted that the two failure exits from the material entry point were different. It therefore proposed listing pin separately: batches would still be passed the same way as before, while pin-related issues would not be described through the same batch-processing exit. The value of this idea was only that the two failure surfaces could be discussed separately; it was not confirmation of a new interface boundary.

Keeping the batch path also had a clear cost. If callers continued to look only at the batch result, their integration would not change because of this draft; but if the split route had already affected the same set of caller samples, maintaining pin separately would create two entry points that needed to be kept aligned. At the time, the callers currently using `namespace reference` had not been identified, so there was no way to determine which adapters would bear this cost.

This gap was never subsequently filled in as a definitive statement. "Lean toward splitting it" in the old document was only a working judgment from the meeting, not a scheduling commitment, much less a change notice to existing callers.

## Constraints before trial use

The draft required both sides to retain the same input set and observation window, changing only the route itself. The purpose was not to chase a green result in a single run, but to avoid treating input differences as route differences. Neither the absence of actual caller samples nor changing only the display labels could substitute for this comparison.

Another more specific stop point was restoration. If exiting could only return callers to the old entry but could not restore the original `event handle`, the split should not proceed. This condition is kept here because it shows that the concern at the time was not that the "new route looked bad," but that the restoration action might be completed only halfway.

The draft records neither a start date nor that a long-term maintainer had taken over. This document therefore cannot state that a trial was run under the constraints above, and no result is available to show that the split route was better than retaining the batch path.

## Traces left in tickets later

RCPA-005 were later used as an entry point for a follow-up review of the record window for the unadopted proposal, but one public note among them says that the expiration action was sent to the wrong ticket and was not from the same incident as this route. That action cannot be read backward as evidence of proposal failure, rollback, or restart.

RCPA-006 only left the first baseline record after the restoration point. They help limit subsequent review to the starting point after restoration, but did not identify the callers of `namespace reference`, nor provide new comparison results for either route. The two tickets are therefore only entry points for revisiting the old draft; they are not enough to support a revised judgment on it.

## The rollback point remains in the old context

At the time, "rollback" first meant restoring the old entry, but the old draft already acknowledged that this was not enough. If event continuity could not be restored at the same time, "the entry is back" could not count as a complete exit. This judgment did not mean that all subsequent integration testing had to continue using the old design; it only set the condition under which that candidate route should not proceed.

Likewise, not finding the callers was not a technical conclusion ruling out the route. It only meant that the affected adapter boundary could not be mapped at the time. If someone later identifies callers currently in use, the impact of the batch path and of listing pin separately still needs to be compared again; the unfinished assumptions on this page cannot be treated directly as a new decision.

## Remaining gaps

- The old draft does not answer which callers were using `namespace reference` at the time.
- If restoration occurred between the two paths, the restoration scope for `event handle` was not spelled out.
- This document does not collate whether comparable caller samples appeared after the first baseline record for RCPA-006.

The material entry point remains `docs/adj-lmcache/proposals/rejected-lmcache-client-integration-approach.md`. This route draft is useful for explaining why it stopped at the candidate stage at the time; it should not be used to announce that a new integration route is already in effect.

# Runtime Monitoring Console Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

This tree preserves the procedure used at the time after a stall was seen through the Runtime Monitoring Console entry point. Here, "stuck" only means that the monitor signals on the page stopped changing; don't conclude from that alone that the operator has stopped, and don't clear the state first. The entry point is still at `docs/adj-operator/runbooks/operator-operations-observability-escalation-contacts-when-blocked.md`.

First, note where the last visible change occurred: did operator-operations-observability itself stop progressing, or could the exit action no longer proceed? If both happened, deal with the exit action first; once it fails, the original display state is hard to revisit.

## Start at the entry point

**The entry point still opens, and monitor still has new signals**

This is not the "stuck" branch. First check whether the new signals have moved past the point where progress stopped; if only the display order is lagging, save the screen as it appeared then and the two before-and-after states, and don't hand this off to the permissions owner. In the old records, someone treated this as a permissions issue outright, then could only work backward from what remained on the page, with no useful decision points recorded.

**The entry point still opens, but stays at the same point**

Look for `eviction pin` in the page records. This term is a lookup cue left by the old entry point, not a recovery action.

- If you can't find it, don't fill in the cause with another guess. Check whether the exit action is still available; if you can still exit, save the location of this stall, then continue from the observations recorded for operator-operations-observability.
- If you find it, check for `namespace reference` nearby in the same section.
- Even if `namespace reference` is present, don't clear the state. It was once treated as a sign that the issue had been pinpointed, but there wasn't enough evidence at the time to show that it caused the stall.

**The page shows only an old state, but the exit action is still available**

Use the exit action first; don't keep retrying against the old state. Before exiting, save the first failure sample you saw and note alongside it how the environment at the time differed from the previous time. An old record includes a retry made too early; afterward, the only thing that could still be confirmed was the last page state. That's why saving the first sample comes before exiting here.

If the page recovers after exiting, don't interpret that recovery as having found the cause. This tree only asks you to record which state the recovery followed. The recovery action has not yet been tried in a shared environment, and the old page did not provide reusable conditions for success.

**The page says you can't open details or continue operating**

Treat this as the permissions branch. Don't use the stall description for operator-operations-observability to make a judgment about monitor or the storage side. What is confirmed is that access to the entry point is restricted; what is not confirmed is whether runtime signals had already been generated before access was restricted. Hand the entry point, the restriction seen at the time, and any exit actions that are still available to the permissions owner; without new confirmation of permissions, the tree stops here.

## The last item in the old branch

When both `eviction pin` and `namespace reference` have appeared, the old procedure checks `backend metadata` last. If that item is absent, the original record requires stopping, rather than going on to settle on the operator, monitor, or exit action as the explanation. Keep this stopping point: it prevents an unsupported line of investigation from being written up as a conclusion about recovery.

Even when `backend metadata` is present, it only means another set of captured data is needed; it cannot replace the preceding page state. Don't reverse the order by looking for it first and then filling in the stall symptoms; that loses the distinction between an initially unchanged display, a blocked exit, and restricted permissions.

## What to leave in the handoff

The handoff only needs three things: whether the entry point still opens, where the last visible monitor signal stopped, and whether the exit action still works. If you've entered the permissions branch, also note whether access was restricted at the entry point or in the details. Copy down `eviction pin`, `namespace reference`, and `backend metadata` only if you actually saw them; don't add them just to make the record complete.

If a second observation is needed for the case, save it alongside the first record; don't overwrite the first failure sample. The old tree did not make the second result a requirement; its purpose is to let the next person know which fork it stopped at, not to treat every stall as the same problem.

This page retains the old entry point and the old assessments. If you encounter a new signal outside the tree, or any step requires new runtime data, stop at that point; don't squeeze related issues back into this tree.

# Quality Signal Dashboard Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

This anomaly first appeared as a very small difference: in the failed samples from test and qa, the CPU fallback differed from the old records. Looking further at the current entry point then revealed two current results under the same object name. Both results were visible on the page, but the information available for tracing them back was not the same. Only after the entry point later separated them did the issue shift from "which state is this same object actually in" to several record-related questions that could be checked individually.

At the start of the investigation, there was not enough material to determine which came first among the execution path, the collection state, and the page timing. The original entry point and its attachments were saved in `docs/adj-csrc/incidents/csrc-quality-signal-board-two-states-for-one-object.md`, not because it inherently represented the cause, but because it still preserved the earliest difference observed. Overwriting it directly with the recovery page would make the original point of comparison disappear.

The recovery page confirmed only that wire round-trip could come back. It can show that one path was able to recover later, but it cannot explain why the caller inventory changed or whether the two current results came from the same stretch of execution. This distinction appeared too late in the initial draft and was later moved ahead of the incident assessment.

```text
test / qa failed samples
        |
        v
Current results with the same name ──> The one with an execution record ──> Actual execution can be traced back
        |
        +----> The other current result ──> Only the page observation can be retained
```

This diagram shows only the investigative relationships between the records. It does not indicate that the two results share an execution process, nor that the one with an execution record is the earlier one. The second result is still part of the incident and cannot be deleted from the source material simply because it lacks an execution record.

## Assessments from the Initial Draft

The initial draft put CPU fallback first because it was the first change that could be compared directly against the old records. This observation still holds, but it did not become a causal attribution. It explains neither why two results with the same name appeared nor why only one had an execution record. Subsequent material did not provide enough evidence to turn the difference into a conclusion about the device side or the execution side, so its place in the incident account is retained here, but it is no longer described as a cause.

The approach of "the current entry point already shows recovery, so the earlier state can be treated as a leftover on the page" was not adopted. The current entry point showed a different current revision at each of two points in time; the final page value can only help identify what is visible now and cannot automatically replace what was saved earlier. In particular, the missing intermediate window cannot be filled in by the last page.

Another claim that once came close to becoming a conclusion was: the two states were merely duplicate displays of the same collection run on the page. This claim was not retained as an assessment either. It did not explain why an execution record appeared with only one of them, nor did it provide an address for linking the other one back to actual execution. Duplicate page displays and duplicate executions are not the same thing.

Therefore, "stop further retries" remains a valid action from the initial draft, but its scope is very narrow. What stops is repeatedly refreshing the same entry point and repeatedly expecting the page to converge; it does not mean stopping new reproduction attempts in qa, nor stopping the organization of records in their original chronological order. Refreshing will not generate intermediate records that were never saved.

## Where the Impact Was Felt

The first impact is regression stratification. The quality signal dashboard needs failed samples to distinguish stable regressions from flaky signals; once two current results appear for an object with the same name, the name alone cannot show which execution a sample corresponds to. If the two results are merged directly, readers will mistake the duplicate entries on the page for repeated actual executions.

The second impact is flaky-signal attribution. A result with no execution record can show that a status appeared at a particular point in time, but it cannot by itself prove that the status was produced by a particular execution. It can remain in the sample set, but it cannot be combined with another traceable result into the same causal chain without verification.

The third impact is an overstated recovery assessment. The fact that wire round-trip can recover means that at least one path is available again; it does not mean that the same-named results have been unified, that the old window now has an execution record, or that the change in caller inventory has been explained. The recovery action and cause confirmation must be considered separately in this incident.

The impact also extends to temporal ordering. The page's current revision is page state, while the time ordering in the original records is a different kind of material. If there is no intermediate record between the two versions, a later split on the page can only reduce the chance of an erroneous merge; it cannot answer what happened during the gap.

csrc · Quality Signal Board has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. This postmortem addresses only test and qa failure samples, regression stratification, flaky-signal attribution, and the record relationships of the current entry. Adjacent projects were not used to fill in the cause, and the page was not treated as proof of execution for other services.

## Incident window

RCPC-011 initially recorded a pending item: "collection status and current entry are inconsistent." It requires separately verifying whether collection is enabled and whether execution is enabled; when the current entry has no evidence, do not fill it in as zero. Here, "no record" cannot be directly changed to "no execution"; otherwise, the blank window would be incorrectly written as a definite status.

On 2 month 17 day, RCPC-011 recorded owner_confirmed. That day's confirmed observation was: there were two current results with the same name, and only one had an execution record. This observation narrowed the investigation scope, but did not identify which result was wrong or specify the order of the two results. It only proves that the two results have different traceability.

Later that day, the maintenance ownership for RCPC-011 changed. The recorded rationale was that the previous person had only helped with triage, so the item returned to the actual maintainer. This was a change in the work entry point, not a technical fix; it cannot make a missing execution record appear merely because of the handoff, nor can it change the content of the earlier page.

On day 18 of month 2, the records showed that the current results with the same name had already been separated, and only the one with an execution record could be traced back. This reduced the risk of misinterpretation at the page level, but the intervening window remained blank, and the alternative address for the execution record had not been filled in as a result either. Separating the results answered "how to distinguish them now", but did not answer "how this happened earlier".

RCPC-009 was later used to mark the unknown window. Its purpose was to keep blank the period between csrc-quality-signal and the current entry point for which no original records existed, rather than infer a history from the summary page. On day 23 of month 2, qa_reproduced appeared on that card, indicating that reproducible behavior had again been observed on the Quality Signal Dashboard side; this is a new on-site observation and cannot automatically rewrite the earlier page window.

The specific gap left on day 24 of month 2 was: after the on-duty person's assignment ended, the alternative address for the execution record had still not been entered. This gap limits retrospective investigation more directly than "whether the page displays two entries" does. Without an alternative address, the result with an execution record can still be investigated through the existing entry point, while the other result remains limited to page-level observations.

On day 25 of month 2, maintenance ownership of RCPC-009 changed again, because the current work mainly involved changes to the csrc · Quality Signal Board core module, with someone on this side taking over. This provided a concrete maintenance entry point for continuing the checks, but did not change the boundaries of the incident evidence. Changes in maintenance ownership and changes in the contents of the records need to be preserved separately.

RCPC-010 was used to align csrc-quality-signal with the current entry point, and explicitly required that the undocumented window between the two record versions be left blank. On day 27 of month 2, the on-site integration debugging work was handed over to a new colleague, and the card was transferred accordingly; on day 2 of month 3, the item moved from To Do to In Progress. This point in time indicates that the alignment work has begun, not that the root cause has been confirmed, nor that the page timeline has been restored.

RCPC-012 retained another check: reorder the current revision and csrc · Quality Signal Board by their original timestamps, using the final page value only as corroborating evidence. This serves a different purpose from RCPC-010. The former deals with existing pages and chronological order, while the latter preserves gaps where no original records exist; collapsing the two into a single statement that "the pages are now aligned" would recreate the original confusion.

## Relationships between the three layers of records

Failure samples are the first layer. They answer what was observed on the test and qa sides at the time, including the difference between the CPU fallback and older records, as well as the reproducible behavior that reappeared later. They cannot, on their own, answer which execution a particular current result corresponds to.

Regression classification is the second layer. It requires a verifiable link to an execution to determine whether a sample is a stable regression, an unstable signal, or an apparent difference caused by a discontinuous recording window. Same-named results without execution records must still be retained because they capture the anomaly as it occurred; but they should not be treated as regression samples already linked to an execution.

The current entry point is the third layer. It can tell readers which revision is visible now, distinguish between same-named results, and serve as a starting point for further investigation. It cannot rewrite earlier windows, turn the final page value into original timing evidence, or substitute for the alternative address for execution records.

These three layers were previously collapsed into a single description: "the state of the same object". Read that way, failure samples seemed to prove the page results, page results seemed to prove the executions, and the recovery page seemed to prove that the historical gaps had been filled. They are now presented side by side so that each layer supports only the conclusions warranted by the available material.

## Retracted attributions

"The CPU fallback difference is sufficient to show that the issue is on the execution side" was not substantiated. The difference remains in the original records because deleting it would alter the evidence from the incident; but it cannot explain why there are two same-named results, nor why an execution record appears for only one of them. Any subsequent reference to this difference can only treat it as the initial observation.

"A newer current revision can represent an earlier window" was retracted. RCPC-012 requires reordering by the original timestamps, showing that the page's final value alone cannot establish the historical sequence. If two page snapshots show different revisions, their differences and gaps should be preserved, rather than choosing one value to speak for every point in time.

"wire round-trip has been restored, so the incident is over" was also split into separate claims. Recovery is the outcome of an action; root cause confirmation is a separate matter. When there is no material supporting the reason for the change in caller inventory, the recovery page cannot answer that question; when the alternative address for execution records has not been recorded, it also cannot be said that all paths can now be traced back.

"The two results are unrelated once the pages are separated" is also inaccurate. They still belong to the same anomaly window and still need to be read together to see that one has an execution record and the other does not. The separation is meant to prevent incorrect merging, not to erase the fact that both once appeared at the same time.

## Recovery actions and stopping conditions

The purpose of retaining the original version of the entry point is to keep the initial differences visible during subsequent checks. Saving the recovered page separately indicates that a particular path became accessible again later; saving unconfirmed items separately indicates that there is still not enough material to link the page to an execution. With the three types of material side by side, readers can ask separately: what was seen initially, which path recovered later, and what still lacks evidence.

Once results with the same name have been separated, follow-up checks should proceed first with the one that has an execution record. This choice only indicates which one currently has an actual entry point; it does not give the other result any additional provenance. The result without an execution record is still retained as anomaly material, but it cannot be used to fill gaps in the execution history.

The stopping conditions for repeated refreshes and repeated executions also need to be distinguished. Indiscriminately refreshing the entry point will not produce the missing intermediate records; qa_reproduced is a new observation with independent value as contemporaneous evidence. Stopping retries does not mean erasing the new reproduction, much less using the new reproduction to explain the old window.

Use of the current entry point is limited to navigation and corroborating evidence. It can help locate the current page, identify the results that have already been separated, and help reveal differences in revision; historical ordering is still handled using the original timing evidence. If the final value on the page conflicts with the original record, preserve the conflict first, rather than rewriting the old record based on the page value.

## What remains unconfirmed

The start and end times of the missing window have not yet been recovered from the available material. The "missing time points" left in the initial draft have not been deleted, because the page split in the month of 2 did not provide the original execution records for this period.

Whether collection was enabled and whether execution was enabled still need to be checked separately. RCPC-011 separate the two because "collection has no records" and "execution was not enabled" are not the same conclusion. Branches without evidence must be left blank, not filled in as zero, and the enabled state cannot be inferred from the green result on the page.

The alternative address for the execution record has still not been entered. After the on-call person's duty period ended, the page already showed the separated results, but the alternative address, the specific entry point for follow-up checks, did not appear along with them. Therefore, one result can be traced back to an actual execution, while the other can still only be confirmed to have appeared at the current entry point.

The reason for the change in caller inventory remains unconfirmed. The difference in CPU fallback was an early clue, while the recovery of wire round-trip was the result of later actions; no material supports a complete causal chain between the two. They can be presented together in the incident's reading sequence, but they cannot be pieced together into a root cause.

The reordering of the current revision and the page chronology is not finished either. RCPC-010 keep the intervening gap blank, RCPC-012 address the original chronological order; one has not replaced the other. The pages have already been separated, which only shows that the current presentation has improved, not that the historical chronology has been restored.

## Follow-up reading order

First return to the original entry point, and look at the first discrepancy between the CPU fallback and the old records. Then check whether the current results with the same name have been separated, and confirm which one includes an execution record. Next look at qa's reproduction records, distinguishing new on-site observations from page remnants from the old window.

When you need to verify the current revision, follow the original-time requirements in RCPC-012, and do not take only the page's final value. If you encounter a gap between the two versions of the records, keep it blank as specified in RCPC-010, and do not backfill it using the recovery page or the later page split.

If you continue investigating the execution side, first look for the alternate address for the execution record. Until the address appears, do not attribute same-name results without records to a specific execution; even after the address appears, still verify it separately from the collection status, the original time and qa reproduction.

RCPC-009, RCPC-010, RCPC-011, RCPC-012 are four distinct navigation points. RCPC-009 mark the unknown window, RCPC-010 preserve the gap between the two versions, RCPC-011 separate collection and execution statuses, RCPC-012 address the revision's original chronological order. Together they describe different cross-sections of the same incident, and none provides a complete explanation of the cause on its own.

## Old notes

The earlier field note only said "CPU fallback was different from the old record," followed by "wire round-trip can recover." These two sentences still have value, but there is no timestamp in between, nor any indication of whether an execution record exists. They are retained here so that readers can see why the initial judgment moved toward the execution side, and why it was not later closed out along that direction.

Another retained short sentence is "why the caller inventory changed is still unknown." It did not become outdated because the pages were separated. Separating the pages reduced direct confusion between same-name results, but did not add any information about changes in the callers. This question must continue to be listed alongside the recovery results and must not be covered over by green output.

Boundaries such as "future implementation is not promised here" were once written too broadly in the old records. The current review retains only the parts that actually correspond to this incident: do not write guesses about adjacent services as the cause, and do not use unsaved intermediate records to fill in the history. Other implementation issues were not expanded here incidentally.

## Review conclusion

This incident confirmed a relationship between records, not a single technical root cause: there were once two same-name current results, and only one had an execution record; the pages later separated them, but the historical gap, the replacement address for the execution record, the reason for the change in the caller inventory, and the original chronology of the current revision have still not all been confirmed.

The quality signal dashboard's regression stratification can therefore treat only results that can be traced back to an execution as bindable samples. The other result continues to be preserved as a field signal, is not reapplied to regression attribution, and is not erased because of the page's final state. Recovery actions, original records, and unconfirmed causes continue to coexist.

# Quality Signal Exit Window Procedure

After the window is triggered, check only the exit actions, the last visible result, and whether the adj-csrc side has completed its required exit actions. Release success still requires separate sign-off from the respective owner; it is not assessed in this checklist.

1. Record the entry point for this run and the last visible result in `docs/adj-csrc/release/csrc-quality-signal-exit-window-checklist.md`. Use the `backend metadata` in old records only as a navigation aid, not as the result for this run.
2. When you see `replay evidence`, preserve the state first. Exit actions change what will be visible afterward. Do not clear it first and document it later.
3. Stop if `release checkpoint` does not appear. The window is still open at this point; do not mark it as finished just because there is no new content.

After the exit actions, check the current record once more. If a new state of the same type appears again, retain the new state without overwriting the last visible result recorded earlier.

Recovery actions for the public entry point have not yet been tried in the shared environment and are not a pass criterion at this stage. Anyone taking over should at least be able to tell which object this run concerns, how far the recorded results go, and why it stopped.

# Quality Signal Exit Window Procedure

Window closeout only handles the exit action for csrc-quality-signal, the last visible result, and the exit action that adj-csrc itself should complete. The corresponding owner's release sign-off is still handled elsewhere; without a sign-off here, do not record the release as successful just because the exit action has been performed.

For this run, take over from `docs/adj-csrc/release/csrc-quality-signal-exit-window-checklist.md`. This file is the record entry point, not the result itself. After opening it, first confirm that you are viewing the record for the current window, not an execution record left from the previous version; the object for this run, the states before and after exit, and the retention location should all be written alongside the current record. Do not simply carry forward a "completed" marker.

## Preserve the current state after opening the window

- [ ] Record how this run's csrc-quality-signal object was identified and the state seen the first time.
- [ ] Leave a sample of the project's own success path and one rejection path. The samples must show that they are from around this window; do not substitute old samples.
- [ ] Mark the first visible result before exit; do not use "normal" or "processed" in place of the actual record.
- [ ] If `backend metadata` or `replay evidence` appears in the current state, first preserve it and the result from that time in the original location, then consider exiting.

RCPC-006 requires checking the two states. First lay them out in order of occurrence, then confirm whether they are the same object. Similar names are not enough; combining states from different objects into one would leave the "last visible result" without its corresponding object. If you cannot confirm that the two states belong to the same object, stop at object verification and do not perform the exit.

## Public entry point

RCPC-007 requires rechecking the public entry point against the original csrc-quality-signal object. Local results can only help locate it; they cannot replace the result from the public entry point.

- [ ] Use the original object to open the public entry point and confirm that it is not another record with a similar name.
- [ ] Leave the last visible result from this recheck; if the entry point is unavailable, the objects do not match, or the result is missing, record the actual situation.
- [ ] If the recheck will overwrite the existing state, preserve the state first; if it cannot be preserved, stop and do not continue with recovery or exit.

The old draft's "The recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment" remains an unverified item. If the public entry point has not been rechecked, explicitly record it as not rechecked; do not rewrite a local sample to say that the public entry point has passed.

## Decide at the window-close point

- [ ] The current record already contains `release checkpoint`; if not, keep the window open.
- [ ] The current object has been verified, and the pre-exit result is still visible.
- [ ] The current result does not use the previous version's execution record; if the source field is empty, do not infer one.

The notes for RCPC-008 indicate that the previous version's execution record has already been marked stale, while the current result has no source attached. Keep these two things separate: the old record may be retained for comparison, but it cannot be moved over to serve as the current result. Finding the on-duty person in the directory does not mean that the actual user has been identified; when the user field is empty, do not use the name in the directory as a substitute for confirmation.

Once the stop point is reached, perform the exit action already in the current record, and record the last visible result after the action immediately next to the pre-exit result. If a new state of the same type appears after the action, stop closeout, preserve the new state, and return to object verification; do not continue to mark the window as ended.

RCPC-008 also requires contacting the original responsible person before the exit action expires. If there is no reply, you may close out using the existing exit action, but the record must retain the fact that there was no reply. No reply is not a sign-off and does not mean that the other party confirmed the release result.

At handoff, pass along only the entry file, the current object's state sequence, and the reason for stopping. Keep the unverified recovery action for the public entry point recorded as unverified.

# Quality Signal Exit Window Workflow

At the end of the window, verify only the exit action for csrc-quality-signal, the last visible result, and the exit action to be taken on the adj-csrc side. The corresponding owner's release sign-off is handled separately; without sign-off, do not fill this checklist in as release successful.

The entry point is still `docs/adj-csrc/release/csrc-quality-signal-exit-window-checklist.md`. Before starting wrap-up, first confirm that the current window record is open, not the previous execution record. The entry file can preserve context, but every window must leave this window's object and result in it; do not merely reuse the old "completed" marker.

This checklist is meant to be followed as work progresses on site; no separate summary is required. It is enough for the object, state order, pre-exit result, exit action, and post-exit result to be comparable near the same record. If any one is missing, do not fill the gap with a later state or an old-version record.

## Lay out the two states first

RCPC-006 records the two-state object check. During operation, first lay the two states side by side in order of occurrence, then determine whether they belong to the same csrc-quality-signal object. Similar state names do not establish that they are the same object; until the object is verified, do not choose either one as the "last one."

- [ ] Write down the object currently being checked and the order of the two states.
- [ ] If it cannot be confirmed that the two states belong to the same object, stop at the object check and do not execute the exit.
- [ ] If they are confirmed to belong to the same object, keep both states in the record; do not retain only the newer one.
- [ ] If the whereabouts of the first state cannot be explained after the second state appears, leave this inconsistency in the record; do not assume that the earlier state has been replaced.

This section handles the object relationship, not the release decision. The later state appearing does not automatically mean that the earlier state is invalid; whoever takes over should still be able to see the original order. Only when the object and order line up do the two results, before and after exit, have a comparable place.

## What to retain before exit

The exit action will change what is visible afterward, so first retain the first visible result before exit, then process the window. The result should correspond to the current object; "normal," "cleaned up," and "returned to baseline" are all insufficient to show what was seen at the time. If `backend metadata` appears in the record, retain it together with the result at that time. It is only an on-site marker; it does not replace the object check or release sign-off.

The old version treated `replay evidence` as the pre-exit retention point; continue using this handling: when this type of material is found, do not clear the evidence first. First confirm that it belongs to the current csrc-quality-signal object, then record its original location beside this record. If no material exists, do not fabricate an entry; if material exists but the object is unclear, do not count it as this window's result.

Recommended items to leave beside the current record, in order:

1. Object identification and the order of the two states;
2. The first visible result before exit;
3. The `backend metadata` or `replay evidence` visible at the same time as the result;
4. The exit action as executed, not executed, or stopped;
5. The last visible result after exit, or the specific reason for stopping.

These items do not need to be organized into a uniform format. What matters is that the before-and-after contents can be compared side by side; a new result must not overwrite the old one, and the action itself must not substitute for a result. If the evidence has already changed and cannot be restored, record "pre-exit result missing" directly and stop; do not infer from the blank after exit that the pre-exit result must have been normal.

## Recheck the shared entry point

RCPC-007 points to shared entry point verification. Recheck the shared entry point against the original csrc-quality-signal object; the local result is for locating only and cannot replace this verification. When the shared entry point has not been verified, record "not verified" only; do not rewrite the local sample as having passed at the shared entry point.

- [ ] Reopen the shared entry point using the original object and confirm that the object shown is still the same one, not another record with a similar name.
- [ ] Leave the last visible result from this verification; if the entry point is unavailable, the object is inconsistent, or the result is missing, state explicitly which situation applies.
- [ ] If the verification would overwrite existing evidence, save the existing evidence first; if it cannot be saved, stop and do not continue with recovery or exit.
- [ ] If the local record and shared entry point result are inconsistent, retain both results; do not rewrite either one as the other.

The old draft's "The recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment" is not a completed item; continue to treat it as unverified. Only after the shared entry point has been rechecked against the original object may the recovery action be saved alongside this window's result; even after verification is completed, it does not replace the release sign-off.

Finding the person on duty in the directory does not mean that the actual user has been identified. When the actual-user field is empty, do not use the directory name as confirmation of the user, and do not write "someone is on duty" as "someone has accepted." The on-duty entry only indicates whom to contact; it does not indicate who vouches for this result.

## Three checks at window close

First check whether the current record already contains `release checkpoint`. Without this checkpoint, keep the window open; do not treat the blank after exit as success. Once the checkpoint exists, check whether the object has been verified, whether the pre-exit result has been retained, and whether the shared entry point has a verification record.

- [ ] `release checkpoint` has appeared; if it has not appeared, do not perform the subsequent actions for "window closed."
- [ ] The current object has been verified, and the order of the two states is still readable.
- [ ] The first visible result before exit is still present, and the on-site marker has not been removed.
- [ ] The shared entry point verification has a result, or is clearly marked as not verified.

The three missing conditions are handled differently: if the object has not been verified, do not execute the exit and return to the two-state order check; if the pre-exit result was not retained, first preserve the evidence that can still be seen, and if the evidence has changed and cannot be restored, record the omission and stop; if the shared entry point has not been verified, the current exit action record may be retained, but the window must not be written as having passed shared-entry-point verification.

All of these stop reasons may remain in the current record. They are not anomalies that need to be covered with a closing phrase, and there is no need to invent a nonexistent result just to close the window. After seeing the stop reason, whoever takes over can still use the same entry point to determine the next step.

## Handling after executing the exit action

Perform only the actions already listed in the current record. After completion, immediately check the last visible result and place it beside the pre-exit result. If a new state of the same type appears after the action, or the state order becomes impossible to explain, stop closing the window: retain the new state, withdraw the "window ended" marker, and restart from the object check.

What is withdrawn is the window-closed marker in the checklist; this does not retract any owner's release decision. Do not skip the new state just because the action has already been executed; the new state may belong to the original object or to another similarly named object, so return to the object check before deciding whether to continue.

Not seeing a new state after exit does not by itself prove that all conditions are satisfied. Still check whether the pre-exit result was retained, whether `release checkpoint` has appeared, and whether the shared entry point has been rechecked against the original object. Completion of the action is one position in the record, not an overall result that replaces the other checks.

## Keep the old execution record and current result separate

The historical notes in RCPC-008 have already pointed out that the previous version's execution record belongs to the old version, while the current result has no source attached. Keep these two things separate during wrap-up. The previous version's record may be retained for comparison, but it must not be moved into the current result; when the current result's source field is empty, leave it blank and stop here, without writing an inferred result.

If the current record contains only the old execution record and has neither the current object nor the current visible result, first mark it as an old record, then capture the evidence again from the current window. The old-version record can explain what was done previously, but it cannot prove what was seen in this window, nor can it prove that the shared entry point or the actual user has confirmed anything.

Handle the original responsible person according to the same principle. RCPC-008 require contacting the original responsible person before the exit action expires; if they cannot be reached, the wrap-up may proceed under the existing exit action, but the record must retain the fact that there was no reply. No reply is not consent and must not be written as sign-off, acceptance, or release completion. If the original responsible person replies later, add the reply separately beside the current record; do not backfill it as confirmation obtained at that time.

## Final review before closing the window

No separate report is needed; review the current record in sequence:

- [ ] The object and the order of the two states are clear; any part that cannot be confirmed still retains its stop marker.
- [ ] The first visible result before exit is still present, and the `backend metadata` or `replay evidence` has not been reduced to a one-line summary.
- [ ] `release checkpoint` has appeared; if it has not appeared, keep the window open.
- [ ] The shared entry point verification result has been retained, or is clearly marked as not verified, object inconsistent, entry point unavailable, or result missing.
- [ ] The last visible result after exit has been retained; if there is a new state, the window-closed marker has been withdrawn.
- [ ] The current result has not borrowed from the previous version's execution record, and blank source fields have not been filled by guesswork.
- [ ] If the original responsible person has not replied, that fact remains in the record.

The items above can close out the exit action on the adj-csrc side. Whether the release was successful is still left to the corresponding owner's sign-off. Whoever takes over should be able to see the object order, the before-and-after results, and the stop reasons directly from the entry file, without inferring the current window from the old execution record.

Even if the window ultimately does not reach exit, leave a record. Object inconsistency, an unverified shared entry point, an empty result source, and missing `release checkpoint` are all specific reasons to stop. When the window is opened again next time, start over from the current object; retain the old-version evidence and the unverified recovery action as background, but do not automatically treat them as a new result or a new pass condition.

# Performance Lab Entry-Point Trace Notes

The entry record's filename is `from-current-entry-to-current-revision.md`. After entering through the Performance Lab knowledge base's public entry point, start at the lab object, then follow the maintenance record beside that object to the revision. "Current" here retains the wording used at the entry point at the time: it refers to the object seen when the record was created, not a claim that later content with the same name is still identical.

I read this file along a narrow path at the time, without bringing in adjacent directories or old output. The two terms that provided a usable trail were `flush interval` and `rollback window`: first find the former in the entry record, then read the adjacent paragraph containing the latter. They only help confirm where you are in the text; they cannot, on their own, establish resource-return or cache-invalidation rules. That relationship was not documented concretely at the time.

`device registry` appeared once. The old record placed it beside a possible branch point: if the entry object directly provides a registry, revision differences need to be investigated further on the device side; if it is merely an adjacent note, the main path still stops at the maintenance record. No direct caller was found in that version, so the registry was not connected to the entry point, nor was the name removed. That judgment remains in its original context; this note alone cannot tell us whether later pages changed the relationship.

When reading the code, first look at the line in the entry file that points to the maintenance record, then search within the record for `flush interval`. Once found, continue only into the local section containing `rollback window`; do not expand the search through similar headings. If two maintenance records give different revisions, note the location where each appears and stop at the first branch point; do not merge the two paths just because the object names match.

A recheck after a cold start followed the same sequence: clear my own cache first, then retrace the public entry point, leaving the shared cache untouched. The resulting observations establish only the entry-point read order and the location of the first branch point, not behavior after clearing the shared cache. `tenant salt` was once written beside the entry paragraph, but there were not enough call relationships to connect it to the revision path, so the old note retained only the term without further explanation.

# Performance Lab Exit Window Procedure

This exit window checks only three things: whether the exit action has reached the required stopping point, where the last visible result is retained, and whether the Performance Lab's exit action has been recorded. Release success still requires separate sign-off from the responsible owner; the checklist does not replace sign-off, and a checkpoint is not a release conclusion.

Start by opening the original checklist entry and confirming that the page is still the record used for this window. If entry names are similar, do not choose based on page color, directory location, or old bookmarks; look for materials only in the entry being used and its existing attachments. If the entry cannot be opened, retain the page information already obtained and stop the exit action at the entry verification step.

## Before Opening the Window

- [ ] Record the exit action that is visible. If the action is not fully documented, leave the gaps as they are; do not fill them from elsewhere and mark the action as executed.
- [ ] Record the location of the last visible result. The result may be in the body or an attachment; note only the location actually seen, and do not treat the existence of an attachment as evidence that the result passed.
- [ ] Confirm that the Performance Lab has its own exit action record. This checks only this side's action and makes no judgment on other release stages.

If the same object has two statuses on the page, first retain the location of each status, then review the on-site notes in DOC-44. Do not delete either item just to leave a single status in the checklist, and do not decide here which status is later.

## Exit Actions

1. Look for `replay evidence` in the body and attachments. If found, retain its original location and the result text immediately next to it; do not extract just this term and remove the stage it describes. If not found, enter "No replay evidence seen" and stop assessing whether replay has completed.

2. Do not clear the working state after seeing `release checkpoint`. This marker indicates that the process has reached the checkpoint, but does not mean the last visible result has been retained or that the responsible owner has signed off. Record the marker, the last result, and any still-missing content separately so later readers do not combine them into a single success record.

3. Check whether `shared-memory wrapper` appears. If it does not, stop the window here: do not proceed with post-exit cleanup, mark this run as complete, or infer that a replacement implementation exists based on a similar name. The existing body, attachments, and checkpoint must still be retained.

4. When all three pieces of material can be found, put the exit action, the last visible result, and the Performance Lab's action in the same record. Here, "can be found" means only that they are visible in the entry being used; there is no requirement to create a new explanation for missing materials, and verbal confirmation must not be entered in the result field.

## Stopping Points and Recovery

Stop the exit action in progress and leave the working state unchanged if any of the following occurs: the original checklist entry cannot be opened, the last visible result is no longer visible, `replay evidence` is missing and the stage cannot be confirmed, or `shared-memory wrapper` has not appeared.

After stopping, do not delete attachments, overwrite old statuses in the body, or change a blank result to complete. Recovery actions have not yet been tried in the shared environment, so this window has no automatic recovery steps. If a restart is needed, first re-establish the assessment from the retained entry, attachments, and filled-in record rather than reconstructing a result from memory.

If `replay evidence` and the last visible result point to different stages, retain both. The checklist does not determine which is correct; the window remains at the checking stage until the maintenance side supplies materials that can be put back in their original locations. If only `release checkpoint` has been seen, treat it as incomplete as well.

## Fields to Fill In

- Exit action and location:
- Last visible result and location:
- Performance Lab exit action:
- `replay evidence`: Seen / Not seen
- Working state after `release checkpoint`: Retained / Unconfirmed
- `shared-memory wrapper`: Seen / Not seen
- Reason for stopping (if any):
- Release sign-off: To be confirmed separately by the responsible owner

At the end of the window, retain this completed record and the attachments already in the entry. If the original command arguments or new rerun materials become available later, append them as new records; do not backfill them as content that had already been seen during this window.

# Compatibility window FAQ

These answers retain the closure criteria used at the time; later explanations have not been added. The recurring questions weren't about whether coordinator-directory existed, but whether it counted as evidence within the compatibility window, who handled the cleanup when a candidate path was withdrawn, and when an item could be marked closed.

**What can the existing coordinator-directory entry point prove?**

It can prove that the candidate path has at least one working positive entry point: the coordinator can hand the request to the directory, and the directory can continue processing it using the object relationships in place at the time. This entry point is not a substitute for full compatibility. After the entry point passes, the negative boundary, cumulative predecessor behavior, and first observation after rollback still need to be reproduced separately; at the time, a single normal result did not count as opening the window.

**Who is responsible for withdrawing a candidate path?**

The agreement at the time was that whoever proposed the candidate path would withdraw it and identify the first observation point after withdrawal. The maintainer of coordinator-directory only confirms that their own entry point no longer references the withdrawn candidate; they do not determine on the proposer's behalf whether other callers are still using it. If the proposer and entry-point maintainer are the same person, they can do both together, but the record should still distinguish between "withdrawing the candidate" and "the entry point no longer pointing to it."

**Under what conditions can an item be closed?**

The wording used at the time was: A work item closes only after its positive path, negative boundary, cumulative predecessor behavior, and the first observation after rollback are independently reproducible.

Here, independently reproducible was understood to mean that the four checks could not use the same path that happened to pass as evidence for one another. A passing positive path cannot substitute for the negative boundary; normal cumulative predecessor behavior cannot substitute for the first observation after withdrawal either. If the unedited pytest node records and environment details were missing, they could be logged as outstanding materials, but the answer at the time did not say that an item could still be closed without them.

**What if only the successful coordinator-directory record remains?**

Keep the successful record without elevating it to grounds for closure. It can still show that the entry point was once reachable and help identify who proposed the candidate path. As for whether it could establish the missing cumulative predecessor behavior, the original answer was that this could not be inferred directly.

# Coordinator Ownership Rotation Decision Record

This rotation discussion did not treat coordinator as a role name that could be handed off abstractly. The dispute centered near the event-ipc entry: who can explain the state visible to callers, and who can only explain the local behavior in the entry file. The meeting record requires naming the public caller first, then stating the precise boundary where the observation changes. Without both points, an ownership rotation only hands off a vague investigation task.

This round's decision is to retain the existing event-ipc entry as the starting point for verification, without treating an entry change as an approved rotation action. The rotation window can remain under discussion, but it may cover only component boundaries already traced through the existing entry. Any ownership change beyond that boundary remains an open item and is not preassigned under the catch-all term "coordinator."

## Scope of the decision

The fixed inspection point is `lmcache/v1/mp_observability/event.py`. Its purpose in this discussion is to provide a reviewable entry point, not to permanently assign the file to a team. The caller, startup path, and event names near the entry let reviewers start from a concrete call and trace a visible state or wire value across an actual component boundary. Retaining this starting point during the rotation means the person taking over does not first have to guess whether "coordinator" refers to the process, the caller side, or the observation side.

This is also the minimum commitment in this round: the handoff covers the relationship segment that can already be followed from a public caller, not the entire multi-process observation surface. The existing material does not support consolidating all event-ipc behavior under a single ownership, nor does it support inferring long-term maintenance ownership from the file location. The entry can still be used by different callers; the rotation record constrains only the observed segment of the state change covered in this round.

One working requirement repeated throughout the review was: "name the public caller and the precise boundary where the observation changes". Here, public caller means the call entry actually reached by the call from Fang Ke, not a role name assigned temporarily in internal discussion. Precise boundary means the point where a state or wire value passes from one component to another and therefore needs to be reinterpreted. If either is missing, the person taking over gets a directory and a guess, not a reviewable area of responsibility.

## Two approaches considered

The first approach is to retain the current event-ipc entry and have the rotation begin with a reproducible caller. The reason to support this approach is not that the entry itself is more important, but that it keeps the discussion within what has already been observed: the call name, startup location, a visible value, and the value's change after crossing a component boundary can all be connected through one reading path. For the quality side, this at least distinguishes two conclusions that must not be conflated: "the entry has been called" and "the downstream observation has changed."

The second approach is to adjust the rotation window first, then use that window to decide which coordinator work should be handed over together. This approach aims to reduce the number of later handoffs and to place the entry, callers, and observation results within one broader area of responsibility. It was not adopted as this round's decision. The objection is not that adjusting the window is necessarily wrong, but that putting the window first would force the review to name boundaries that have not yet been traced. Once the name is fixed first, a later discovery that the observation changes elsewhere can make the ownership description look complete while still leaving it unable to answer what the caller actually saw.

The reservation is recorded here as well: the current entry may not be the only entry for all related calls, and the location in the file may not be equivalent to the actual component boundary. Adopting the first approach does not make the second approach worthless; it only removes the latter from this round's decision. If a new caller or a new state-change point is found later, its relationship to the existing entry should be stated separately rather than retroactively folded into this rotation conclusion.

## How ownership is expressed

This round does not use "entry owner" to cover all subsequent interpretation. For the portion where the caller and boundary can be confirmed, the side responsible for interpreting the public interface provides the call semantics. For the portion where it can be confirmed whether the observation is sufficient for a quality judgment, the quality side retains the review judgment. The responsibilities are adjacent, but they are not merged. The former explains where a value becomes visible; the latter explains whether that value can support the current judgment.

This arrangement is intended to avoid two common misreadings during a rotation. The first is treating the name at the startup point as the person responsible for the entire execution chain. The second is treating the appearance of an observation value as proof that it has been interpreted the same way downstream. The first would cause the new owner to take on an undefined scope too early; the second would cause the quality judgment to skip over where the change occurred. The existing evidence supports recording these as separate matters only.

The review-approved investigation order remains: start from the reproducible caller and the fixed entry, follow only one observable state or wire value, and once the actual component boundary is reached, restate what that value means on the other side of the boundary. "Restate" does not mean completing a system diagram for every handoff; it means not carrying an observation from before the boundary over as a conclusion about after the boundary. If the value has not changed, or there is not yet evidence showing where the change occurred, the rotation description should stop at the confirmed call segment.

## Conditions for reconsidering the rejected approach

For the window-adjustment approach to return for a decision, at least two local facts must be added: which public callers are included in the window, and at which component boundary the observation changes for each caller. Listing more files or more coordinator names is not enough, because it still would not show whether the added portion extends the same relationship or mixes another behavior into the rotation.

In addition, if later inspection shows that `lmcache/v1/mp_observability/event.py` is only a forwarding point, the rotation record should retain it as the starting point at that time while recording the new change boundary separately. The original conclusion reached from that entry must not be erased just to make the ownership map simpler; it remains valid within its scope, but no longer carries the broader interpretation.

The conclusion of this round is therefore narrow: retain the current event-ipc entry and hand over the confirmed portion according to the public caller and the state-change boundary; do not treat the window adjustment as a decided action. The rejected approach and the reasons for rejecting it remain attached to this record so that the next discussion does not assume the window has already been approved.

# Operational Image Switch Handoff Procedure

This staging image refresh will not be handled as "replace the image first and fill in the record later." First enumerate the known consumers of object-key and count the old entry points. Only one consumer that can roll itself back may try the candidate path first. The handoff must retain the original input, the repository state at the time, the location of the first difference, the responsible module, and an executable rollback action.

Keep the old entry point until the trial run is complete. After a consumer switches from the old entry point to the candidate path, first verify whether the same object-key can still be recognized by the original entry point; when the first difference appears, stop there and do not move any other consumers over. The difference record must show whether the input changed, the image changed, or the operator's handling of that input changed.

The consumer using the candidate path performs its own rollback: restore the old entry point, bring back the original input, and confirm that the old path is usable again. The next person taking over may schedule the next batch only after the caller count, first difference, and rollback action have all been recorded. Consumers that have not yet been verified remain on the old entry point.
